utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor. Good morning all others. If I could remind you, Doctor, of the affirmation you took at the beginning. Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and good morning, Your Honours. Examined by Ms. Somers: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rudolf. Good morning, Counsel. Mr. Rudolf, yesterday -- I'll just try to bring you back to where we left off. If you'll excuse me a second I'll just ask my colleague to give you the last question so we can pick up. We had begun, Mr. Rudolf, to discuss the events of the 6th of December, 1991, and we were following some of the entries in what has been referred to as the harbour-master's log. I will ask you about some of your conversations, if any, with the JNA once it became clear to you that in fact Dubrovnik was under attack on the morning of the 6th of December. First, however, I'd like to return to one point and ask you: When you were tasked originally by Zagreb to come to the Dubrovnik area to carry on what have been described as comprehensive negotiations to put an end to the hostilities, among other things, you indicated that you had been informed that you would be meeting with General Strugar. Had you ever had any dealings prior to that time with General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received instructions on the 29th of November, 1991 to go, together with Ministers Kriste and Cifric, to Dubrovnik. I had never seen General Strugar before that. I am seeing him for the first time in the Court today. Nor did I have any meetings with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you: Did the term "2nd Operational Group" have any particular meaning to you at the time, at the end of November 1991/beginning December 1991? Did the term have any meaning to you?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to Cavtat and you found Admiral Jokic there instead of General Strugar, was there -- did Admiral Jokic say anything to you about the fact that General Strugar was not there? Alternatively, did you express the view that you were to have met with General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Admiral Jokic did say that Mr. Strugar was unable to come. However, it was absolutely a matter of indifference to me to whom I would be speaking, the general or the admiral. What mattered to me was that it be a representative of the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it your perception when you were negotiating on the 5th of December, 1991 that Admiral Jokic carried authority to -- of the Supreme Command and of General Strugar to carry on these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did have authority. In fact, when we met, and before we started discussions, we introduced ourselves as representatives of the Croatian government, whereas Admiral Jokic, as the authorised representative of the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces of Yugoslavia introduced himself. These introductions were made before the beginning of discussions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Despite the fact, if I understood correctly, that there was one point concerning inspections at sea that was not firmly arrived at, did you continue to believe that Admiral Jokic had the authority from General Strugar and from the Supreme Command to carry on these negotiations when you left Cavtat on the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection. I object, Your Honour. The evidence and the testimonies of the witness is that in his understanding Admiral Jokic was a representative of the Supreme Command and had authority from the Supreme Command. Nothing he has said so far indicates that my learned friend may, for the second time now, link up General Strugar into her question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You had better deal with that, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I will ask accordingly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, when you learned that you were going to deal with General Strugar but found you were going to deal with Admiral Jokic, were you satisfied that Admiral Jokic was there in place of General Strugar, for whatever reason?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told in Zagreb when I spoke to General Raseta and later when I spoke to the office of Admiral Brovet, that I was going to speak to General Strugar. When we arrived in Dubrovnik on the 4th, we established contact with Sofronije Jeremic and we agreed to have this meeting in Cavtat. I believe he said we would see Admiral Jokic, but as I said, when I arrived there, what mattered to me was to speak to a representative of the Supreme Command. I didn't care which.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you satisfied that Admiral Jokic was taking the place at that time of General Strugar, for whatever reason?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was convinced that Admiral Jokic represents the top leadership of the armed forces of the JNA. He just said that General Strugar was unable to come, and it was sufficient to me to have a counterpart who was representing the Supreme Command of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was the contingent from the ECMM inside the negotiating room on the 5th of December? Did they come inside the negotiating room or did they remain outside?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure enough to answer this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving back to the 6th of December, I'd like to ask you if the -- now, yesterday we went through some of the entries and particularly I had asked you about an entry on page 20 of what is I believe P162, the log.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I may ask the usher to leave perhaps in front of Mr. Rudolf a copy of that exhibit, as well as presenting to him the document from tab 11, which is P136 also, but it's in tab 11 from our binder. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, yesterday -- actually, beginning on page -- it commences a bit earlier, it starts on page 18, runs to page 19 of the log and goes on to page 20, discussing various points that were proposed by -- in a communication to you from Boka VPO, as it says, from Admiral Jokic. Point 7, in particular, was asked of you, about the blockade of the town. Can I ask you, please, to turn your attention to the second document, which is marked at the top P136. It is a transmission from Admiral Jokic to the Crisis Staff and to yourself, dated the 6th of December. And it also contains -- well, first of all, do you recognise the contents of it? I mean, it's in evidence, but I just want to know that you're sure of the contents of it.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, does this document summarise the points that are in the log from pages 18 to page -- actually, the very top of page 21? Is it the same -- effectively the same transmission? If you look from page 18 through 21 of the log and you look at this document, the separate document, is it effectively the same transmission?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. Yes, it's the same message. The difference is that it's handwritten in one document and typewritten in the other. I believe it is the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you take a look at the typewritten document at point 7, there's a reference to deblock -- do you see it? To deblock the town completely?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to withdraw the weapons that jeopardise the town out of shooting range. Now, which weapons -- from which side is it your understanding that this is referring to? Whose weapons were jeopardising the town?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 5th, we had discussions. We demanded that the JNA withdraw from the territory of the Republic of Croatia, as had been agreed in Zitnic and in Rijeka. However, the admiral not only did not accept this, he refused to discuss this option at all. He demanded on his part that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. armed forces withdraw from Dubrovnik, in exchange for a withdrawal of the JNA to a larger distance from Dubrovnik. In other words, he suggested a demilitarisation of Dubrovnik in exchange for a withdrawal from Dubrovnik to a greater distance. When the armed forces of Croatia withdrew, although it was promised that the JNA would not come into Dubrovnik, they did, and occupied the town. That's what we talked about with Admiral Jokic. He especially insisted that mercenaries withdraw from Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question, though, being very focused, because time is not working with us today, the point 7 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, regarding interpretation, if you allow me. On page 6, line 3 and 4, Mr. Rudolf talked -- said that although it was promised that they would not come into Cavtat, not Dubrovnik, and they did come into Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me answer your question. It is very understandable. It says here that the weapons that represent a danger to the town should be withdrawn out of shooting range, and then in a sort of exchange --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose weapons? The weapons from which side?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understood this document, the weapons that were a danger to the town meant weapons of the JNA, and from the Croatian side armed forces should withdraw from the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were there, to your knowledge, mercenaries in the Croatian or on -- among the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment when Admiral Jokic spoke about mercenaries, I didn't know whether there were any or not. However, as soon as our negotiations were over and when I went to Dubrovnik, I made inquiries and established that there was only one foreigner, precisely from Holland, a man who married a local woman from Dubrovnik. He was practically a Dubrovnik man of Dutch origin, a man who had a local wife. There were no other mercenaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, would you -- were you suggesting that the only sticking point was the place of inspection of vessels, that other than that, it appeared to both sides that the agreement was a done deal?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness is being led. He hasn't said anything so far about which points are in issue and which are not; at least, I haven't heard him say anything to that effect. Maybe my learned friend heard something else. Where exactly has the witness said what was controversial in the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I will go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Ms. Somers, you're catching the condition that Mr. Rodic and Mr. Petrovic have had of imagining what's in their mind is in the evidence when they're cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you will have to watch it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, what was -- if any, what was a sticking point that -- well, were there any points that were not completely resolved when you and the JNA side left Cavtat on the 5th?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had agreed immediately after initial negotiations, where I explained the situation in Dubrovnik and presented our demands and then Admiral Jokic did the same. But we immediately agreed on one thing; to cease hostilities, to cease with the fighting. And then ensued a discussion about the reopening of local roads and daily services between Dubrovnik and the surrounding islands, that electricity should be restored to Dubrovnik and the water supply. We even talked about the Dubrovnik-Split road being opened. And the only issue we couldn't resolve was the issue of the naval blockade of Dubrovnik. Right at the beginning, Admiral Jokic said that he was not authorised to discuss or agree to a lifting of the blockade, because that's what we insisted on, and we had no success, and then we started looking for a compromise. We proposed that if the blockade were to remain in place, the checking of the ships should be done in the Dubrovnik port of Gruz, whereas the admiral insisted that ships should be checked or inspected at sea. We insisted on the port because it was the month of December, and when you inspect the ships at sea and when the weather is bad and the sea is not calm, then a ship had to go to the port of Zelenika for inspection. That, of course, was a great inconvenience, both to the crew and to the passengers, and I, as a minister for maritime affairs, had received a lot of complaints from various crews. We had a captain of the Slavija ship, for instance, who was Montenegrin and who complained about this. We had to replace him. That was the only open issue that remained unresolved, because the admiral said he had to consult the Supreme Command. We said: Fine, we will talk to our government as well. And we said goodbye to each other, with the conviction that we had reached agreement about the most important issues, that is, the most important issue, and that is a cessation of hostilities. And we had also agreed to come back the next day, at 10.00, and sign this agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any particular perception about whether or not -- as to the other points Admiral Jokic had the authority to enter into agreement? You indicated one point, the inspection was left open, but were you satisfied that as to the other points, the authority was vested in the admiral? You shook your head, but I don't think they pick it up.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I think on all other issues he was authorised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we did go into the beginning of what occurred yesterday on the 6th of December. I would ask you if you can tell us: Did you have, once you became aware of the attacks in Dubrovnik on that morning, did you make contact with the other side, with the JNA side? If so, how did you do it, from where, and with whom did you make contact?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was awakened by the shooting, and then I went down to the bar, just as everyone else seemed to do. And we could see clearly that Dubrovnik was being shelled. This bar and restaurant and this room where the ECMM monitors were sitting faced the sea. You had a very good view. I'm sorry, I'm not a soldier, but I was later told that the weapon used was some sort of Maljutka. You could see clearly the shells flying over and landing near the ships in the city port. I told you yesterday that I was absolutely devastated when I saw this, because I couldn't believe that despite the agreement we had reached only a day before, Dubrovnik was being attacked. I was absolutely crushed. I didn't care about staying alive even. All my hopes were crushed, because that hope had arisen only a day before, I told you. Our communication with the town and the communication with the defence of the town was still in place, and I went to call Admiral Jokic immediately. I dialed the number, I say, but I don't know where he was located, whether it was Kumbor or Herceg-Novi, but we could not get him on the phone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- can you tell us, please, what instrument you used to reach him. How did you try to reach him? With what?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: By telephone, the telephone which was at the hotel. However, Mr. Di Mistura showed up then. He was right there and he had a satellite phone in his room. Then we all went upstairs to try to get Admiral Jokic on that satellite phone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he was the one with whom I had agreed on a cease-fire the day before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Who is Mr. Di Mistura?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Di Mistura was the representative of the United Nations in Dubrovnik. He had a suite of rooms in the hotel and he had a satellite phone. There were representatives of all kinds of international organisations in Dubrovnik at the time. They were all in the Hotel Argentina. Whenever I say anything about events on the 6th December, I'm speaking about Hotel Argentina. More specifically, about this little Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. annex building attached to the hotel. It's connected to the main building. It's one and the same hotel. So dialing this number, using this special phone, we finally got the office of Admiral Jokic. I spoke on the phone and I said: Is Admiral Jokic there? They said no. And then I said: Look, you are attacking Dubrovnik. And the man on the other end of the line said: No. We are not attacking anyone. Then I took the receiver and turned it away from me and then the man on the other end of the line heard the shooting. It was something horrible. And then he said: Okay. I'm going to get Admiral Jokic now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the man on the other end of the line was?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you indicate at the time -- I'm sorry. Did you indicate to the man on the other end of the line that the Old Town was also implicated?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I simply said that they're shooting at Dubrovnik. When one says Dubrovnik, it means the entire city. After a certain period of time, I couldn't tell you exactly how long, maybe 20 minutes, maybe half an hour, I got Admiral Jokic on the line. I don't know whether I called or he called --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that they're shooting at Dubrovnik and it means the entire city, does that include the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there came a point where you did speak to Admiral Jokic himself?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you tell Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I immediately said to him: Admiral, they're shooting at Dubrovnik. Yesterday we agreed on a cease-fire. And I also put a receiver so that he could hear the shooting, to which he replied that they did not issue an order to fire at Dubrovnik. He said that it was ludicrous, ridiculous, to do something like that. He said that they were investigating what was going on, and what was most important for me, he suggested, a cease-fire to me, a truce, to begin at 11.00. I naturally accepted that immediately. I can state to you here again that, as you know, I'm a professor of international law and such agreements can be reached on the phone. So we agreed that the cease-fire was to start at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you indicate to Admiral Jokic that Dubrovnik and the Old Town were under attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness has already answered this question, several minutes ago, and in a very clear manner. Please take a look. Page 11, line 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was with the other individual that I had made reference to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you carry on, please, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, my question to you was: Did you indicate to Admiral Jokic that Dubrovnik and the Old Town were under attack? Do you remember what you said?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, that was what, 12 or 13 years ago. I think I said that Dubrovnik was under attack. When you say Dubrovnik, that includes the Old Town as well. I can tell you that we could see everything that was going on from Hotel Argentina, and we could see that the rounds were landing on the wall ramparts, wall ramparts of the Old Town on the south side. We could also see that within the Old Town there was a smoke rising after the explosion. So it was clear that it was under attack. The rounds also landed on the Hotel Argentina. One round landed on the annex in which we were --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you convey this to Admiral Jokic, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, did you have any communications with General Strugar that day?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you -- first I'll show you some documents and then I'll ask you. Perhaps it frames better the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I can ask that tab 12, the document from tab 12, which is P23, be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is what appears to be a fax, addressed to you. Do you recall receiving this communication on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this is a faxed message. Yes, I remember. I received this sometime in the afternoon. I think that it was stated that the general had sent this fax sometime at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would you indicate, please, what it says in that fax. Would you be kind enough to read it out, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I read it out or shall I interpret it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... read it.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the top here. I think it says: Telegram from the VPS, which is naval military sector, the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik to Minister Rudolf Davorin. "This morning, JNA forces were fired upon." And then I can't really read what it says here. I think, "with mortars and machine-guns from Srdj and Babin Kuk, without provocation. Our forces returned fire in response to this action. However, upon my orders, the unit ceased fire at 1115 hours. However, your forces did not abide by the cease-fire. It can therefore be concluded that the buildings in the old heart of Dubrovnik are being damaged by the fire your forces are laying down. Commander, Colonel General Pavle Strugar," and then something else at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you -- in pieces we'll look at this. In the first part, where it says "This morning JNA forces were fired upon with mortars and machine-guns from Srdj and Babin Kuk, without provocation," did you at the time agree with that assertion by General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Second part: "Our forces returned fire in response to this action. However, on my orders, the cease-fire at 11.15 -- the units ceased fire at 1115 hours." Do you agree that the JNA forces returned fire in response - in response - to Croatian provocation?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that there was a cease-fire put in place at, it appears, 1115 hours?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with the assertion by General Strugar that your forces did not respect the cease-fire, and it can therefore be concluded that the buildings in the old heart of Dubrovnik, or Old Town, are being damaged by the fire your forces are laying down?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your reaction to this particular communication by General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I received this message from General Strugar, I consulted -- I don't know exactly what time it was in the afternoon, but I consulted, as I always did, the commander of the Dubrovnik defence, Mr. Marinovic. I told him what was stated here. He said it was not true. Yesterday I told you what was the attitude of this lieutenant general of ours, lieutenant colonel of ours. He was a true soldier, and I don't think that he would dare say to a minister something that wasn't true. So he immediately disagreed with the contents of this message. As to the cease-fire at 11.15, this is true. We initially said the cease-fire should begin at 11.00, and then another radio message arrived stating that it should begin at 11.15 in order to inform all of the units that were on higher elevations. We agreed with this new cease-fire at 11.15, and it started -- it started coming into effect step by step, because the fire was being reduced in intensity. As for this final claim of colonel general that it is our forces who are destroying the Old Town, to tell you the truth, I believe this to be complete nonsense. I don't know whether that day or the following day Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I watched TV and heard that another general of the JNA - I think his name was Gvero - had stated in Belgrade that Croats were setting on fire tyres near the ramparts of the Old Town to create an impression that the JNA was attacking the town. Naturally, such claims, I knew immediately that they were not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, you were there. How would you describe the attack on the Old Town which you observed? My question goes to whether it was constant, continuous, sustained, sporadic. Can you give a description of it, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of that started in the morning. We established contact immediately with the commander of the Dubrovnik defence forces, and we were told that all of that had started early in the morning by the fortress Imperijal on Srdj mountain and later it spread to the town. When we arrived at the bar and when we saw what was going on, we saw that the entire city was under attack. And it was fascinating to watch these rounds that were fired hit the ramparts, and it looked as though a mosquito was attacking this huge structure. And these shells were landing on the left side, on the right side, and I didn't believe that the rounds would hit this ship, because the ship was that of the parliament, but at one point, a shell hit the ship on the right side, and if you look from the Hotel Argentina on the town, you see the view which is the usually depicted view of Dubrovnik. So we saw the ramparts and we could see the fire rising on this side, on that side, from the shells that were exploding. The shells were landing all over the town, around the hotel, in front of the hotel, on the road in front of the hotel: Later on, we could see the empty shells of the rounds. So the entire town of Dubrovnik was shelled, and I would depict that shelling as a brutal one. The shelling continued until the cease-fire came into effect. I can tell you that we were fortunate to have a satellite telephone there. We established contact with Admiral Jokic. We concluded a cease-fire. I don't know what would the fate of Dubrovnik have been had we not managed to do that. So this was a continuous, brutal attack from the Hotel Argentina. I can tell you that the Zarkovica and other hills were behind our back. Therefore, we could see the rounds flying towards Dubrovnik, and we could see the smoke rising up. When the cease-fire came into effect, this shelling was reduced gradually, and then what happened was that - I don't know who told us, was it the president of the municipality or somebody else - that nine buildings were on fire. The night was approaching, and this was a sight that one can never forget. The night was approaching, there was no more electric power, and behind, in the Old Town, we could see fire raging there, ablaze. We called Croatian government and asked that Italy intervene in order to provide assistance. Some six days prior to that, I was in Rome, and I negotiated with Italians. I even established contact with -- between Bari and Dubrovnik. I asked the Chef de Cabinet of Mr. De Michelis to send us the planes that could put the fire out. However, the citizens of Dubrovnik managed to put the fire out. I think that a fire-fighting ship from Korcula had arrived, and it helped in putting out the fire in the Old Town. So this happened on the 6th. This tremendous, brutal attack. I can tell you that at one point, with Mr. Di Mistura, I watched from his small balcony the rounds landing in Dubrovnik. I met with a gentleman on the 5th, in the evening, and he asked me whether I believed the JNA and that they would put in place the cease-fire, and I replied yes. And as we were watching this sight, I remember that I said to him: Well, sir, we have lived in the same state for 70 years, and now look at this. And then I used this impolite word that I do not want to use here again, and I said to him: Now look how they are destroying this peaceful, beautiful town from above. Several days later, after the cease-fire was concluded, Di Mistura asked me again: Do you believe the JNA now? And I said no. And I -- it should have been the other way around. I should have said no first and then yes later. Later on, when I was Croatian ambassador to Italy, I met the gentleman again and we would always go over these memories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry to cut you off, but time again is marching against us. You witnessed, as you indicated, this shelling which you described as brutal. Did you -- you mentioned you saw the ramparts being shelled, the ramparts of the Old Town. Did you witness shells going to other parts of the Old Town or any explosions going into other parts of the Old Town; edges, middle, any parts of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Behind the ramparts is the Old Town. I didn't see what shells were landing, but they were landing behind the ramparts in the Old Town, and we would see the smoke, the smoke rising up, here, there, in various places, which means that the shells were landing --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see it going on the inside?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, behind the ramparts, which is inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it maybe is not clear to the record when you say "behind the ramparts," so I want to make sure it's really clear.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Behind the ramparts in the Old Town. Let me just give you a detail: When we came back on the 5th from Cavtat, they proposed to us to move into Hotel Dubravka, which is in the Old Town, because prior to that we were staying in Hotel Argentina. The night was approaching so we said we would remain in Hotel Argentina. And that day, on the 6th in the afternoon, they came to wish me a happy birthday, and then what happened was that in the room where I was supposed to sleep, a shell landed in that room, which is in the very centre of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you observe, during the course of the attacks on the 6th, any JNA attacks from the sea? What was your observation, if any?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the issue of fire-fighting, I wanted to ask you about. You mentioned the need to put out the fires. And if I could ask you to turn to the radio log -- the harbour-master's log. I just wanted to see if there's -- on page 25, if I could ask you to take a look, please, at the harbour-master's log. Do you see it, sir? Page 25. And it has an entry for 1813 and 1831. It says: "For the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff: Lieutenant General Pavle Strugar has given permission in principle for a tugboat with a water cannon to enter the old port of Dubrovnik to put out the fire. We ask you to let us know in due time about the number of ships so that we can create conditions for their safe passage." And then it bears a name, Lieutenant General Pavle Strugar, with a "message relayed." Do you have any further information about the permission granted for the tugboat to come in? Is there anything further you can elaborate on about this?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the tugboat did arrive, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to give us an approximate time when you consider the attack against the -- against Dubrovnik and particularly the Old Town to have ended on the 6th of December? If you can give a rough time frame.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think roughly at around 5.00 in the afternoon. Because it was gradually diminishing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you able to indicate or are you confirming that the fires that you observed did continue to burn perhaps even on to -- did they continue to burn even the next day?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not on the following day, but after 5.00, yes, into the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the particular reason why you -- why a request was made of the Italians to put the fires out?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my idea. A few days prior to that, I was in Rome. I had discussions there on cooperation and so on. And it seemed to me -- you know, that sight was a terrible one, so it seemed to me that it would be a good idea to ask the Italians to put out the fire. You know, at the time, Croatia did not have those fire-fighting aeroplanes, and I doubt that we could have gotten assistance from anyone else. I even called the Deputy Prime Minister, Granic, and I think that we received a consent from Italians to assist us. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I would ask -- may I ask the usher, please, to distribute from tab 15 of the document. It is from P61. It was tab 33, but in this particular binder it appears under tab 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, do you -- you indicated that you had -- you've read to us the communication received from General Strugar that day, on the 6th. Do you recognise -- do you recognise a document that says it is from you to General Strugar, also dated the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you compose this particular communication?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you do so?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received the message from Mr. Strugar where it was stated that it was us who caused the attack, that we were in fact destroying the Old Town, and I thought that we needed to reply to that. So I wrote this letter and sent it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at any point subsequent to this letter receive any communication from General Strugar about the content of this letter?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The following day, on the 7th, before we commenced negotiations in Cavtat, Admiral Jokic gave me the letter from Mr. Strugar. I took it to be a reply to my message.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, was in the -- what content was in this particular letter?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That letter stated that he also said he regretted the attack, and he said that there was a renegade unit of the JNA and that unit carried out the attack. He said that he had ordered this to be investigated and apologised. I gave this letter to everyone, everybody read it out, and I think I gave it even to Mr. Hvalkof, the gentleman who was there representing the European Community. We were all on one side of the table. So I received this letter from General Strugar, and after that we had no further contacts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you take this communication from General Strugar to be an acknowledgment or an admission that one of the units of the JNA had in fact initiated the attack and had carried it out? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, listen. I didn't know then, I still don't know now what was happening on the other side and who started the attack. To me, it looked like a synchronised attack, going from one side of Dubrovnik to the other side. Now, whether this was one renegade unit which started attack without authorisation, I don't know that. In fact, I never learned what was going on on the other side. I even planned to go to Yugoslavia, to Serbia one day, and talk to Admiral Jokic, ten years following the event, to see what actually took place on behalf of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, you have written a book about the war in Croatia, and does part of it -- what is the name of the book that you wrote about the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The War We Did Not Want."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you write this book?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you discuss this particular communication from General Strugar in your book?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you, if I -- just to -- if I present a copy of the page, may I ask you just to read what you wrote at the time. And I'll just distribute, so that the Chamber can see it. Of course it is in the Croatian language, and I'll just ask that it simply be read out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the page please be put on the ELMO for the benefit of interpreters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, was this book a book that was put out to the general public? Was it a commercially printed and distributed book?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you can indicate, if it's on the ELMO, be good enough to -- I'm sorry. Is it on the ELMO? The ELMO is the projector next to you, Mr. Rudolf. If you could turn the next page, please, that gives a little bit of information about -- okay. And then the next page, please. Thank you. What is the date, if ...? Sorry. The book does in fact have a date of publication. Could you indicate that date, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next page, please. Does this page indicate the conversation -- or the communications with General Strugar that you've had on the 6th and the 7th?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. On this page, I listed messages of the 6th, and on the next page, messages of the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could you turn to the next page, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what -- could you indicate where you have made reference to a communication from General Strugar that you indicated you received on the 7th. If you'd be kind enough to read it into the record.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is right at the top of the page. "The next day, the 7th December, before the second round of negotiations, Vice Admiral Jokic handed to me in a blue envelope the response of General Strugar, wherein he gives new interpretation of the attack on the city of the 6th December. He wrote that one unit of the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, made a movement on its own initiative and opened fire. And he also expressed regret over what he called 'the incident that occurred.' He informed me that he would start an investigation and establish who was responsible."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am fully prepared to tender it if it would assist the Court. Otherwise, if the record is sufficient, I can leave it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the record is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rudolf. Can we go back now -- we've finished with that particular page. During your communications with Admiral Jokic on the 6th, did Admiral Jokic ever indicate to you any concern about outgoing fire from the Old Town of Dubrovnik? Did Admiral Jokic ever indicate to you as you were speaking to him or otherwise communicating, any concern about any outgoing fire from the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at any time during the 6th of December observe any outgoing fire from the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to observe any outgoing fire from any areas outside of the Old Town but in close proximity to the Old Town, if you were in a position to see?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I was able to see, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, please, to take a look at tab 9, the document in tab 9. This document dated the 8th of December is from what institution, or what stamp does it bear and is it addressed to yourself, Mr. Rudolf, to you? Is it addressed to you?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the stamp of the command of the Dubrovnik defence headquarters, and the report was addressed to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall having absorbed or read the contents of this report?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I received a sea of these reports, but I see this description here and I think they sent me this as an explanation of what was going on, and I later transmitted it to the government. Judging by this stamp and the contents, I believe this letter was handed to me. I only can't remember when or --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you can just take a very quick perusal through, because of time, and point out a couple of things to you.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In particular, there is a paragraph on the first page which discusses the type of weaponry involved in the attack. Was this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. consistent with what was discussed or what you came to learn about the weaponry? And if you're not familiar with that type of detail, feel free to say so. Your hands went up. I assume that you don't want --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I'm not familiar with this. You see, I'm no soldier. I keep making mistakes about generals and admirals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No problem. Moving on to the section where it says, "The fiercest fighting took place between 0900 and 1000 hours when the enemy directed all artillery pieces to fire on the Old and New Towns, which inflicted serious damage on the Old Town," do you concur with that? You were observing. Is that --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it was the fiercest phase then, I don't know, but it was a continuous attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Reading down, it indicates above where paragraph 2 begins, it says, "There were no naval or aerial combat operations." Do you concur with that?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did not see any. Well, that would be all we needed, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the balance of it deals with certain indications of some of the damage on the last page. I will not necessarily ask you to go through it, but if you could confirm, if you know, that some of the buildings that were damaged did include the church of St. Blaise, the Franciscan monastery, the church of St. Joseph, the Sponza palace, the archives, the Rupe museum, the convent of the Sisters of Sigurate, and the Stradun. If you could just indicate if you're in agreement with, if you're in a position to say ...

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 6th, we were unable to leave Hotel Argentina at all. It was impossible because the road leading to the Old Town was under fire. The next day, however, we did leave the hotel and we went straight to the Old Town, because those parts next to the Old Town had been shelled but the devastation was not too great. In the Old Town, the picture was terrible. In the Stradun, the high street, that is, there were shards of glass, debris. The building where the Dubrovnik festival was held was damaged. And I will say again, nine buildings in total were either destroyed or burnt. I was together with Pedja Sehovic, who was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "in total," totally destroyed, in their totality destroyed?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Completely, completely destroyed. Nothing remained of them, only the walls. And Mr. Pedja Sehovic and I -- who was a writer, and I toured all this. We saw a shell had hit the library, destroyed the fences. Damaged buildings were very numerous. They were destroyed either completely or partially. One of them was the Franciscan monastery. But I will tell you one more thing: We had agreed for a commission to come, precisely based on the letter that I addressed to Mr. Strugar, where I invited him to come to the town and see for himself. And some people indeed from the Yugoslav People's Army came to the town, and they filmed all this. The picture was inconceivable. It was a terrible sight. And in one of these documents that you gave me to read, it says 14 people were killed, 14 civilians, and 30 were hurt. I believe there were more casualties. That's only on the 6th. In addition, 19 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- other people were killed, including four soldiers. That happened on the 6th, when those people were killed. We toured the hospital, everything. You know how these things are done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to see the bakery which baked bread for the town. We tried to cover all of Dubrovnik to give some encouragement to people. People had come out into the streets to try to tidy up a little. But at that time, the cease-fire was in place and it was quiet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd ask to move this document into evidence, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be P164.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry to interrupt this examination, but I'm concerned about the time, because we need time to examine the forensic witness, the forensics expert. Could we be apprised of the plan for today so that we know how we're going to proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We certainly can, Mr. Petrovic. We propose to adjourn in about ten minutes, resuming at about a quarter to 11.00. As the first witness will be yours, Dr. Lecic, we would propose that you should have a full 40 minutes to deal with the evidence of Dr. Lecic, in addition, of course, to her report. It will be for you to decide how best to divide that between examination-in-chief and re-examination. The Prosecution will have 40 minutes to cross-examine, we will have a short break, and then Dr. Matthews, as that is the second witness of the Prosecution, we would propose 25 minutes for the Prosecution, to be divided as you choose between examination-in-chief and re-examination, the Defence to have a full 40 minutes to cross-examine Dr. Matthews. And that will take us to just on a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm sorry again that I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I had in mind making that clear before we broke so that each of you could plan your time, but we tried there to allow both sides a reasonable opportunity, but also to give as much time as we feasibly can to Dr. Rudolf today. I've been over this before and I won't go over it again for the unfortunate Dr. Rudolf. Yes, continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And thank you for clarifying that for the parties on the timing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the particular communication that you indicated General Strugar had sent to you that you mentioned in your book? Do you know where the actual document may have perhaps ended up? What did you do with it?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We sent all those documents on to the Croatian government in Zagreb through the municipality of Dubrovnik. I managed to make photocopies of only the most important radiograms, and they are published in this book. And by the way, this book can be bought in Belgrade as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from -- other than General Strugar, are you aware of any other official, high-ranking officer of the JNA, who has blamed the Croats for the shelling of the Old Town in connection with the 6th of December? Did you hear it from General Kadijevic, from Admiral Brovet?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only mentioned General Gvero. I remember that name very well. On the radio, in a public statement, he accused Croats of setting fire to the town themselves by burning tyres and creating an impression that Dubrovnik was being destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear from Admiral Jokic that he believed the Croatian forces had shelled the Old Town themselves?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to take a look at the cease-fire agreement that you had entered. I just want to find the tab. Actually, if we can take one moment. There are several documents that I would ask you to address. In tab 13, they're a bit loosely put together so I'll direct everyone's attention to the ones I'm interested in showing to the witness. They're the documents bearing ERN 03091857 in English, dated 7 December. The next document in English is 03091853, which is also dated 7 December. And the next document 03091852, dated 7 December. And the last is 03091854, dated 7 December. Mr. Rudolf, if we can take a look first at the document that is -- it bears in the upper right-hand corner in the English 03091857. And perhaps put it on the ELMO. I think it might be helpful, please. The Croatian language version is 01076138. Were you able to find it?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If Mr. Usher can assure that it's placed soundly on the ELMO. I think the witness has it in his hand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, do you -- well, you have the Croatian version. Do you recognise this document? Did it come from you?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's dated 7 December 1991 --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you indicate, please, what -- if you can very quickly run through the content of it - to whom it is addressed and what the concern in it is - we'll try to get through this very fast.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had agreed to negotiate in Cavtat, to hold final negotiations. However, when we arrived on the 5th December, on the first day, when we went out on the coast, we found soldiers lined up at a distance of ten metres. They looked very unkempt. Some of them were unshaven. They held these automatic or semi-automatic rifles. And when I was supposed to go into town, I called the general and I said that I had the impression that our life was going to be put in danger, that we might be attacked. And we agreed to meet in Srebreno, which is some way between Dubrovnik and Cavtat. Admiral Jokic accepted this, and the next day we used the hydrofoil to reach the port of Srebreno. However, the vessel was not able to put in because it was -- because of the way it was built, so we had to go to Cavtat anyway. Admiral Jokic asked us where we got the information that somebody was planning to try to kill us, and we said that it was no particular intelligence, that it was only our impression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said a few moments ago that you called the general, "and I said that I had the impression our life was going to be put in danger," to which general were you referring? Just to clarify, please. To which general?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To be quite clear: I made this mistake again. I sent this message to Vice Admiral Jokic. He was the only one I communicated with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, does this, then, reflect the concern that you had about your security, and for yourself, and was it also for the other ministers involved, the other negotiators, members of the negotiating party? Is that a yes?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask, please, to have this document admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received. Ms. Somers, can I ask how much longer you would expect your examination-in-chief to be with Dr. Rudolf?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It will not finish, clearly, today. I would anticipate less than one hour, less than one hour. And I regret that I will have to -- I know we have to bring the witness back, but that should be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I cannot help feeling sympathy for the position of Dr. Rudolf, but things are beyond our direct control. You have been what I would call messed about, and I'm sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's possible, I had pulled a few documents out -- are we stopping now or at 10.30?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If we're resuming at 10.45, there must be at least 20 minutes for the tapes to be changed, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Fully understood. I'll pick up with these at our next meeting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So we need to break now to enable the people who are interpreting to rest and the machinery to be prepared for the next session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can I just quickly give the number to the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, we will now adjourn the hearing of the evidence of Dr. Rudolf until Monday afternoon. My understanding is that it's Monday afternoon. That's shared by one of the members of the Chamber. The other member fears it may be Monday morning. So would you please all check with the court officer, and we will resume at a quarter to 11.00 with the hearing of the evidence of Dr. Lecic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor, and welcome. Thank you very much for coming. If you would be kind enough to take the card and read the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you could be seated, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Petrovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor Lecic.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, for the record, tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: My name is Dusica Lecic-Tosevski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you are professor of psychiatry at the medical faculty of the University of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I teach at the medical faculty as a professor of psychiatry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that in 1992 you got a Ph.D. on the subject depression and changes in personality?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: My Ph.D. is in psychiatry and personality disorders, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you are now working as a manager of the Centre for Education and Mental Health in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. That is where I work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you the founder and long-time member of the Stress Clinic in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. In 1994, I founded the Stress Clinic, the first clinic of this type in our country. I was its director in chief until year 2000, and since then I have been a consultant there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a founder and coordinator of the Centre for the Rehabilitation of Torture Victims?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. In year 2000, with a group of my associates, I founded the centre for rehabilitation of torture victims and I was its coordinator until year 2003. This centre was supported by the European Commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among numerous other papers enumerated in your CV, which is attached to your report, did you also author a textbook New Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, co-authored this textbook, dealing with specific personality disorders?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. This book was published in 2000 in Oxford.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This textbook I have mentioned, is it a reference book in the area of psychiatry in Europe?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. That is the reference textbook in this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please enumerate some of your functions in professional associations, professional psychiatric associations, that you discharge at this time.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I believe I listed them in my CV, but what is most important perhaps is that right now I have been for a number of years president of the prevention section of the World Psychiatric Association. This association covers 120 national associations. I'm also a member of the working committee of the World Psychiatric Association.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Lecic. I would now like to move on to the subject of our discussion today. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Did you compile an expert report on the health condition of the accused, Pavle Strugar, earlier this year?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. In January of this year I drew up a report on the health condition of Mr. Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell us: Which diagnoses were you able to establish in Mr. Strugar?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be best to say in which way I reached them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I had the opportunity to do several things; namely, to examine in detail the medical reports that were attached on the condition of Mr. Strugar, and as far as I remember, there were 18 of them. So I gained an insight in his previous treatment by my colleagues, and then I did a general psychiatric examination, evaluating his mental status. I took so-called hetero data, I talked to the family of Mr. Strugar, and then I applied modern specification and used several instruments in putting my diagnosis. Since there is no distinct line between somatic and psychiatric or mental health, it would be best to tell you first about my insight into the physical health of Mr. Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, only outlines, because we have your report.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Most notably, there are almost no organs -- there are -- that are not affected practically. He has chronic renal insufficiency, with history of coxoarthrosis. Almost all his joints are affected. He has coxoarthrosis of the lumbar spine, associated hypertension, in fact, oscillation of hypertension, and he receives medication for this. He has also lung problems. Those are the main diseases. There are a number of others, such as benign prostatic hyperplasia. The illnesses I established are recurrent depression, that is, recurrent depressive episodes. There are four of them listed in the specification. Then residual PTSD, as well as vascular dementia, which used to be referred to as multi-infarction dementia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please try to slow down a little, because a considerable part of what you said is not being recorded efficiently. You have mentioned these three diagnoses concerning the mental status of Mr. Strugar.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please: What is the interaction of these diagnoses? What is their influence on his overall health condition?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: As I have already said, since there is no clear line between somatic and mental health, all the previously listed conditions, especially renal insufficiency and vertebrobasilar insufficiency, which is a consequence of the damage to the spine, practically affect the three psychiatric types of diagnoses that I established, because a person is not a collection of fragments, a person is one whole. So all of these symptoms that he presents and manifests are both mental and somatic and physical and lead so a considerably diminished ability to function. Do you want me to elaborate?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just wait a second for all of this to be recorded. Please be kind and, in addition to everything you've just stated, could you please give us -- say to us what are the consequences of increased levels of creatinine and urea in Mr. Strugar's body.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: When I examined him, pursuant to findings that I received at the Detention Unit, he had increased levels of creatinine and urea, as well as a bacteria called pseudomonas aeruginosa, he had fatigue, exhaustion, and all of these are consequences of chronic intoxication of metabolites of renal functions which are chronically increased in the patient. He has the diagnosis of chronic renal insufficiency, which sometime in the past brought to -- led to an acute worsening of his condition, at which point a laser intervention was performed and this renal insufficiency was so grave that it endangered his vital functions. And if you allow me, I will add that he has a chronically increased function of renal metabolics, they are consistently increased, and they normally lead to metabolic encephalopathy, or reduction of mental functions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give it to us in layman's terms? What does that actually mean?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: That means that he is not able to participate in normal vital functions. He has a reduced mental ability, acuteness, a reduction of -- reduced attention span, and this is something that is caused by his other illnesses, this recurrent depression that I've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Lecic, could you please tell me: How do changes in the levels of urea and creatinine influence the condition of the patient? To what kind of consequences does the change in levels of these two elements can lead?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Well, this is difficult to forecast. As far as I could see, the changes are of a permanent nature, because he has a permanent intoxication of these two elements. And since he has a chronic renal insufficiency, it is to expect that, in addition to frequent infections, these functions will be deteriorating in the future and he will also -- he might also develop an acute renal insufficiency if this condition is not treated. So the increased levels of these two elements have negative consequences on the patient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us about the other two diagnoses that we heard you mention here; PTSD and the depression. How can you describe the situation with respect what you were able to diagnose in this patient?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: The recurrent depression that Mr. Strugar suffers from leads to numerous symptoms: Inability to sleep. He has insomnia. He is passive. He has lost interest in many aspects of his life. He is apathetic. He has a disorder in his attention span and also in his memory. He started forgetting important events in his life, which is also something that is caused by vascular dementia. And since there is also a residual PTSD disorder, he also started forgetting certain traumatic events in his life, whereby he is actually protecting his brain from unpleasant memories, which is very typical for a PTSD reaction. So all of these conditions and illnesses lead to a significant reduction in his concentration, attention span, and his memory, including remote memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us: In addition to clinical interview, what other tests have you applied in order to reach these diagnoses, and also could you tell us something about the application of the test Impact Scale of Events, which has been discussed here before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: As I've already said, I used clinical and psychiatric interview, which is the gold standard for reaching diagnoses, as well as criteria for DSM-IV classification. I've listed the criteria in my report, and especially the ones that have been met by this patient in order to reach the diagnosis. However, in order to confirm the diagnosis, I further applied several other tests, diagnosis of general symptoms, Symptom Checklist Revised, which has a group of nine symptom clusters. And in addition to that, I also used the Beck Depression Inventory test and also Hamilton Depression Rating Scale. These were applied for measuring the stress and depression. I also applied Impact of Events Scale, which was designed by the associates of Mr. Horovitz [phoen], and also another subtest intended to measure the level of stress. What I would like to say about these tests is that these are standard tests used in diagnostics and research. There is a longer version of the test called Impact Events Scale Revised. We use that as well, however, we also sometimes apply a shorter version of this test, which can only be said for the Hamilton scale, that it comes in two versions. So the Impact of Events Scale is a test that is widely used in research throughout the world, and despite the fact that there are many other scales used for measuring PTSD level, it has been established that this particular test, Impact of Events Scale, is very reliable, has a very high level of reliability in psychiatric research. And this test is used by two institutions in Europe which are studying the PTSD levels in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. refugees. One of the researches started by these institutions started in 2002, and the other one started in 2004, and they are aimed at studying the level of post-traumatic stress. This is supported by the European Commission and seven countries participate in this study in Europe, including four countries from the Balkans. Pursuant to our diagnostic protocol, this is exactly the test that we used, the Impact of Events Scale. Three months ago, I had a work published in an American Journal of Personality Disorders, and in that article, it was stated that this test, Impact of Events Scale, is very relevant for measuring the level of trauma.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us something general about the use of tests when making psychiatric diagnoses in addition to psychiatric interviews. These tests that are used, are they the most important, the basic or the most reliable source for reaching conclusions and findings about the subject that the psychiatrist is studying?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Since in psychiatry we try to make our findings as objective as possible, yes, we do make frequent use of these tests. The interview is considered to be a gold standard in psychiatric research. In addition to that, we use various classifications, such as DSM-IV, which is typically used in the United States and which I have used. This is the DSM-IV classification that I have used in reaching my findings. And also the tenth international classification used by the World Health Organisation. These tests, as I've said, are very important in order to objectivise our findings and in order to measure the disorders, and also so that we can follow the changes in the condition of our patients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When reaching your diagnosis for Mr. Strugar, did you also receive measurable confirmation in the tests that you've applied?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. There were no discrepancies between the various means that I applied, including these various tests that I applied, the DSM-IV and others; they've all confirmed the same diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the diagnoses that you made was vascular dementia, which used to be called multi-infarct dementia, pursuant to the old classification. Could you please tell us: When a patient is standing trial and when he has to attend trial for four or five hours five days a week five months in a row, could you please tell us: How does this affect the ability of the accused to participate and to follow the trial against him?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Vascular dementia, which used to be called multi-infarct dementia, is one of the numerous illness that the patient has, as I've said. Since this affects small blood vessels in the wide mass, which is linked to the hippocampus in the brain, which has to do with the memory function, this affects the memory of the patient, attention span, concentration, ability to understand at a high level what is going on. Mr. Strugar does understand where he is. He used to be a very intelligent and very successful man. However, what is important and which shows that there was a significant deterioration in his intellectual abilities as compared to his condition previously. This leads to a reduction of his ability to participate at a high level in proceedings that are this important. My impression was that Mr. Strugar feels as an outsider in this trial against him. In addition to that, he is passive and dependent, but I think it is important to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will get to that later. But this is the answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I would just like to add: When I spoke about the PTSD, the residual, chronic kind of it, and the depression, although these conditions are psychiatric, they also have a biological aspect, and they can impair the structure of the hippocampus and can lead to impairment of memory. What should also be said is that when all these illnesses and conditions are combined, as was said in an article published in American Journal of Psychiatry in March of 2003, this all leads to an increased risk of suicide. Mr. Strugar has stated several times that he has had suicidal thoughts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, very briefly, what is the difference between his ability to understand certain concepts and the dementia? How does that affect his ability to follow trial? How do these two things differ, these two conditions? How do they affect the ability of General Strugar to follow trial?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: He certainly understands where he is, what is going on, what he's accused for, and partially understands the consequences of these proceedings. However, he is not able to participate actively in the trial itself because he has an impaired memory. He only has a partial memory of things that take place during the day, as well as the events that took place earlier, because he has an impaired short-term memory and he is not able to participate actively at a high level in a sophisticated proceedings of this nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If somebody forgets things frequently, how can that person plan his or her defence? How can such a person develop his or her strategy and long-term planning?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Strugar can do that only with great difficulty. I saw that he was able to anticipate the consequences of his actions. Right now he's in a passive, dependent stage or status. He said several times, "My life is in the hands of my attorneys," which shows that there is a regressive and infantile attitude to his activities, which is typical for vascular dementia, especially for a person of his advanced age. Therefore, as I've already said, I do not think that he is able to participate and to function in a trial of this nature, especially at a high intellectual level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that a person who forgets things in a way that the patient does, do you think that such person can successfully testify before this Trial Chamber, and can this person be cross-examined without negative consequences?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I do not think so. The interview with General Strugar was not an easy one, especially because he has an impaired hearing and constant ringing noise in his ears, and also because of his forgetfulness, despite the fact that he tried very hard to create an impression of a great man, a man who controls his actions, he was not able to conceal this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were able to see the reports written by your colleagues, who were hired to do so by the OTP, and I would like us to go over them, but very briefly, please. One of the theses contained in these reports is that the accused is able to plan the strategy of his defence, to plan the strategy of his defence. What were you able to see yourself?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I was unable to see that General Strugar has any kind of strategy for his defence. My interview with him lasted nine hours, and during the interview, he manifested a high level of forgetfulness, as I've already said.
