He was passive, he looked dependent and helpless, he was unable to anticipate, to anticipate future events and consequences of what he was doing. Rather, he was in a passive state and dependent upon his lawyers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned a minute ago, but it wasn't recorded in the transcript, that he even tried to remember your name, but was unable to do so during the interview.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I asked him about that. He also manifested a disorder called dysnomia, inability to name objects, persons. At one point he even forgot the name of his favourite grandchild. Therefore, he used to be a man who could control his activities, he was a man who held high posts, and this inability causes him to feel extremely irritated and unhappy; and I saw that my colleagues reported this in their reports as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In their report, your colleagues agreed that the diagnosis of Mr. Strugar is vascular dementia. They say, however, that it is a mild form of vascular dementia. Please be so kind as to tell us: Is there a relevant international classification, meaning, specifically, the DSM-IV, the classification of the World Health Organisation, that recognises distinction between mild, medium, serious, or other vascular dementia?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Vascular dementia is an organic thing, so it is diagnosed in a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. categoric way. Either there is or isn't one. It is not a multidimensional thing. These terms can be used in diagnosing personality, for instance. In the tenth international classification, which all psychiatrists are duty-bound to use, there is no distinction between levels of dementia. There is depression, which can be complicated or uncomplicated; there is depression -- or rather, dementia, which can be combined with depression or not; as well as depression which accompanies delirium as a disorder of the consciousness, or mild forms of madness. However, there is no mild or serious form of dementia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have two more questions for you, Dr. Lecic. In fact, I have many more, but there is no time, so I have to be happy with two. Namely, the influence of diagnosing various disorders and the suicidal potential derived therefrom.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: On several occasions, General Strugar said that he would commit suicide and that he had intended to do so before but he is not doing so because of his family. In speaking to them, he minimises his troubles and he's trying to create the impression of a strong personality. And he explicitly asked me not to convey this to his family so that they wouldn't worry. I believe that his various conditions and diagnoses, especially the co-morbidity of his diagnoses, can lead to such an act in the future.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question to you, Dr. Lecic: Could you tell us something about your observations regarding General Strugar's personality. How do you evaluate his personality?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I believe that evaluating a personality is one of the key things in diagnosing in psychiatry. Different persons manifest clinical symptoms in different ways, including the symptoms that we have discussed today regarding Mr. Strugar. Mr. Strugar is first of all a patriarchal personality, which he manifested in his behaviour in the prison. He is used to being a hospitable man, so he apologised to everyone for not being able to be a better host. He is a man who strongly believes in the truth and believes in justice. And he has obsessive traits of personality. What does this mean? He is inclined to perfectionism. He is very strict towards himself and others. He is inflexible in relation to ethical values which he abides by rigidly. He is a highly controlled person and he has a constant need to leave an impression that he is a strong person. Another trait of his is negation of problems, denial of problems, which makes diagnosing all the more difficult. But if we go deeper in evaluating his personality, especially the psychiatric problems that he denies, we find isolation of the affective side. What does this mean? Although he displayed in the course of the interview a certain degree of emotional instability and oscillation of emotions, and even became tearful, he suffers from alexythymia, inability to express emotion, and by definition such individuals are inclined to developing psychosomatic orders and to somatisation of his problems, which is precisely what's happening with him. I would also like to add that Mr. Strugar, in his desire to be very self-controlled and to come across as a strong man, minimises his problems and dissimilates. Dissimilation is a psychiatric term which means that he is diminishing the importance and size of his problems, which is in keeping with the structure of his personality and with his earlier record of functioning. However, all these traits, which of course dominate in him, are significantly modified by his passive, dependent behaviour caused by the existing conditions and his present status.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Lecic, for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps later I would like to have another three minutes in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Petrovic. Your timing is precise. Yes. Mr. Re. Mr. Re may ask questions of you for the Prosecution. The lectern. Cross-examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is not the first time you've given evidence before the Tribunal, is it?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is in fact the third time I'm testifying before this International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on each of the three occasions, you have testified for accused people facing charges before the Tribunal, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I have testified for the persons for whom I have been called to testify. [In English] I'm sorry. I was witnessing for the persons for which I was invited to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you wish to speak to me in English? Would that be easier to conduct this?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's entirely up to you. Whatever language you are most comfortable in. You just broke into English there.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Choice of language? English?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: English, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. -- sorry. Professor, the other two were, of course, the case of Stevan Todorovic and Damir Dosen, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, they were, the two of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stefan Todorovic, you gave evidence in sentencing proceedings, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Sorry? In what kind of proceedings?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sentencing proceedings.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with Mr. Dosen, you gave evidence during trial for him prior to his pleading guilty to persecution.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in each of these three cases you have examined -- you and other psychiatrists have examined the same accused, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And each of these three cases, you have diagnosed post-traumatic stress disorder in the accused, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In each of these three cases - Todorovic, Dosen and General Strugar - the other psychiatrists haven't. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, the Trial Chamber in the case of Dosen, which is the case of Sikirica, disregarded your findings because there was a conflict between you and Dr. Skolja, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the conflict regarding Mr. Dosen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the case of Todorovic, the Trial Chamber likewise did not take into account your findings of post-traumatic stress disorder in sentencing Mr. Todorovic, did it?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I'm obliged to my profession, and I didn't follow what the Trial Chamber decided later on. What I was aware of, that my colleague who was engaged by the Prosecutor, colleague from Germany - I'm sorry, I don't remember his name - did not diagnose post-traumatic stress disorder but was also -- didn't -- was not involved in the questions related to the subject which I was explaining witnessing here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The issue was whether he had diminished responsibility or diminished capacity at the time he committed the acts for which both pleaded guilty, and in both cases, Todorovic and Dosen, you found they had post-traumatic stress disorder but the other psychiatrists expressly didn't; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. But I am -- I should add once again that the other psychiatrists were not dealing very much with stress and post-traumatic stress, which is the area of my expertise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you examined Mr. Dosen, you also administered the same barrage -- tests that you administered to General Strugar, didn't you? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. These are the tests that are usually given to psychiatric patients, most of them, especially those who have experienced some kind of trauma.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You weren't, of course, assessing Mr. Dosen's capacity to stand trial and continue with the proceedings, were you?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: No, I was not. It wasn't a question that I was asked. I was asked just to evaluate his psychiatric condition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The thing I suggest that is in common with your examination of both General Strugar and Mr. Dosen is that you administered basically the same two tests for both; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, these tests are administered to most of traumatised patients and in the studies and in the Centre for Rehabilitation of Trauma Victims, which I coordinate, we always administer the same tests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also, of course, diagnosed Mr. Dosen, who was a shift leader at the Keraterm camp, as having a "passive and dependent personality," didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I didn't. I don't have the papers here, but I didn't say that he was passive/dependent personality disorder. He has -- he did have passive, dependent personality traits due to his high anxiety that he was manifesting at the time of the examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could quote directly from your summary and conclusions in the publicly filed document filed by Mr. Petrovic: "The accused Mr. Dosen had dependent personality disorder, combined with passivity, compulsive traits and conforming lifestyle."

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me, but I really can't remember what I wrote two years ago. Dependent personality perhaps, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a -- is another way of saying that a passive, dependent personality?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: If you want to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object to this type of questioning by my colleague. First of all, it has nothing to do with what we are discussing here today. That's one. And I am astonished by this approach, because I don't see of what assistance it can be to the Trial Chamber. Second, all that my learned friend is mentioning was done more than three years ago, if I remember correctly. If he wishes to ask questions about all this, he should present here both what Dr. Lecic wrote at the time, namely, her report, as well as all the other documents that he is referring to, because at this moment nobody can any longer remember what happened three years ago. I am the first to admit that I can't remember what was written, what the details were, and what terms were used. So if he wishes to continue this line of questioning, I would appreciate it if he would put before Dr. Lecic her report so that we can see what the condition of the accused Dosen was three or four years ago, if that is relevant at all. Dr. Lecic would then be able to read her own formulations and she can answer these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I've actually moved on from that point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm glad, Mr. Re, because this Chamber is certainly not going to consider the accuracy and reliability of earlier diagnoses by the professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're concerned only with this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The point of that question will become apparent right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, during your examination-in-chief by Mr. Petrovic, you described General Strugar as having a passive, dependent personality. I can't find that in your report. Can you show me where it is in your report, that diagnosis?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I didn't say that he had passive/dependent personality in his report -- in my report, but that he has passive position, and that he passively relies upon the Defence counsels, that he has a passive and helpless position due to the decline of his overall functioning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my note of your testimony here was that you said he had a passive and dependent personality.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Passive and dependent position, and regressive movement, actually regression from the previous superior functioning to the helpless position that he is now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your curriculum vitae, you refer to a book you wrote called "The Stresses of War," written in 1993, co-edited with Pedrag Kalicanin. This book, of course, was written from the Serb perspective, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: That is the only perspective that could have been used because we presented what was happening in the -- with the people we were working with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You wrote it in 1993, and the chapter you co-authored was titled "The Misuse of Medium and Psychiatry in the --" Sorry. "The Misuse of Medicine and Psychiatry in the Satanisation of the Serbian People." That was the chapter of --

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that you complained about or you referred to Croatian journals making references to a Serbian personality trait.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Actually, that journal was something we used to show that psychiatry should not be misused because psychiatry is a science and not impassive discipline. And in that journal, many non-violate conclusions, non-scientific conclusions were used. That chapter and that book was quoted and is still quoted in American scientific bases, databases called Biosys, and has been referred to by many colleagues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is what you said in your chapter: "In the religious, ethnic, and civil war waged in the former Yugoslavia, medicine and psychiatry in particular are being misused in order to spread hatred against the Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object. I would like this book which is referred to to be put before the witness so we can see the entire context, to see what is written, how it is written to enable the witness to answer. I don't see what purpose can be served by quoting one sentence if questions are to be asked on the basis of the document to which my learned friend is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness shows no sign of lacking familiarity with the work for the general questions, but I take it you're about to move on, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I certainly am, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Are you getting to the merits of this particular case soon?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you working between 1996 and 2001? There seems to be a gap in your curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: No, there's no gap at all. I was working where I am working now, at the Institute of Mental Health and at the School of Medicine, University of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the history which you have provided -- sorry, detailed in your report, you haven't sourced all of the information there, have you?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The history which you have detailed relating to General Strugar comes from a mixture of sources, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: The history mainly comes from General Strugar himself, and the part of the history comes from the -- very small part, from the informants, and interviewing the informants as a role in psychiatry, it is called so-called -- the so-called third ear in psychiatry. We always have to consult someone in order to be able to make a proper diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You obtained information from General Strugar, his wife and his son. Are those the three sources?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, as well as from, as I said before, from a lot, a huge pile of medical reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of interviews, the three sources were the wife, the son, and General Strugar? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Strugar is, of course, aging and unwell and is missing a husband.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, and what's your question related to that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's difficult for her to see him, where he is and where she is.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I don't think it's difficult for any wife to describe her husband and his behaviour in their life, which was quite long life together. And the question she was asked was to describe how she sees the personality of her husband, which is, as I said, a must in psychiatric diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. My question relates to her speaking to you. You spoke to her this year. She was in the former Yugoslavia and he was here; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that stage, she and -- it would be fair to say both she and her son wanted General Strugar home, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Obviously, as every person does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you explore with those two people whether General Strugar understood the nature of the charges and the case against him? Did you ask them?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Not very much, but I did ask what was their feeling about -- not feeling but attitude regarding the memory and the problems and the health of General Strugar, because I am a doctor, and I have --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not asking you that, I'm asking you specifically about the matter before the trial, which is the capacity to understand the proceedings. Did you ask them or speak to them about his awareness of the charges or his consultations with Defence counsel or any of the matters concerned with the conduct of the trial?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I did ask the son, who told me that his father was having severe problems with memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm speaking specifically about the trial.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask them such a specific question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree, of course, that neither the son or the wife could be considered to be particularly objective sources of information about their absent father?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: The family, the social context, is considered to be very objective, and when psychiatric diagnosing is being made, and as I said, and I need to repeat it, it is the third ear in psychiatry, and they were objective and they -- as much as any science, including this one here today, can be objective in describing the previous functioning of the husband and the father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your diagnosis or noting a decline in emotional control, was that based on the history you received from Mr. Strugar's wife?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: It was also confirmed by Mr. Strugar's wife, but this was something I observed and I received that information in the interview with the general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You only met him once on two days. You had nothing to judge it against except a history from his wife. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: The emotional discontrol?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The decline in emotional control. Your only control test was the wife, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: He was the one who told me also how strong he was, and he was apologising for crying on a few occasions when interviewed by me. That's one thing. And another thing is: Psychiatrist's duty is to diagnose personality traits of a person who is being diagnosed in order to be able to make a proper diagnosis and prescribe a proper treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll please ask you to just concentrate on what I'm asking you. I'm asking you about the control test being the wife and him. Look, have you -- how many people have you dealt with who have been incarcerated?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I've dealt with many people in the Centre for Rehabilitation of Torture Victims, people who were detained before they came to the centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many assessments have you provided in relation to a defendant's capacity or fitness to provide -- sorry, to be tried?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I've provided many assessments as asked by United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees when they wanted to prepare their cases for resettlement to the third countries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That wasn't what I asked you. I asked you about specifically about fitness for trial. That is accused people. How many accused people have you assessed --

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Not many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I was only asked for this case to respond to that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you said "not many," are you saying to the Trial Chamber that this is indeed the first assessment you have ever made of someone's capacity to stand trial as an accused person?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But I was, as I said, someone who was asked for many assessments of psychiatric condition and personality of many traumatised people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you appeared in sentencing proceedings, providing psychiatric reports for people who are being sentenced before, apart from Mr. Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you visited prisons in Serbia, where you reside, and treated prisoners who are facing trial?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I have visited prisons in Serbia on many occasions, and I have lectured at prisons in Serbia. And I'm also a member --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, no. Stop. That's not what I'm asking you. Have you treated prisoners, not lectured at prisons. Have you treated prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I was just going to tell you. Let me add what I was going to say. I have not treated prisoners in prison because it's not allowed for --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I want to hear.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: -- anyone who is not working in prison, but I need to add that I'm member of the International Committee for Education of Prison Doctors, residing in Norway, and I have to add that I have written a chapter, which is going soon to be on the Internet, of treating mentally disordered people in prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, to my question: Are you saying you have never treated prisoners before?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I can't treat prisoners since I'm a professor of psychiatry and professors are not working in prisons in our country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree that responses to incarceration - that is, prisoners - could be - I just want you to answer yes or no - depressed mood?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Incarceration is one of additional factors, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prisoners may suffer depressed mood as a result of their incarceration; you would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I would agree with that, but that would be only one factor, because each illness is multifactorial and not monofactorial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Loss of appetite is something that prisoners experience?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, he told me so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about General Strugar, I'm talking about prisoners in general. That is the response of people who are incarcerated. Please confine yourself to that. Prisoners can suffer disturbed sleep patterns?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: It depends on the personality, and some even might go to sleep much longer, to develop what is called hypersomnia, or even to have increased appetite as a defence and a coping strategy with the situation of incarceration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prisoners may also become emotional when talking about or thinking about absent family, mightn't they? Or that's fairly typical, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it's fairly typical. It also depends on the personality. Because we have to judge by the individual cases, not to generalise such a serious matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say you wouldn't know whether it's fairly typical because you have no experience of dealing with prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I have not experience in dealing with prisoners as a physician of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. prisoners, but I do have experience because I have read widely and I'm a professor, I teach these things to my students, and I examine them. They have to pass exams responding to the questions like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from General Strugar, have you ever dealt with any elderly incarcerated prisoners? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Obviously not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that prisoners may suffer suicidal thoughts, especially in relation -- especially if they're facing a long sentence?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Some prisoners, yes, but not all. One can't, again, generalise these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your report, you referred to the -- I withdraw that. You've already told Mr. Petrovic that you write and publish in English, and you're giving your evidence in English, and you've, of course, published a chapter in the major English textbook, the New Oxford Textbook on Psychiatry. You have quoted a test in your report which is the test you say you are using to determine competency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I didn't say it was the test for competency. I never said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have your report in front of you, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At page 14, last page, Fitness To Stand Trial, it says: "By definition 'defendants facing criminal trials need to understand and participate in the proceedings. Psychiatric disorder can render a person incapable and unfit in relation to trial. The defendant should be able to follow the proceedings and be able to instruct lawyers so that defence can be made. The defendant should have capacity to fully comprehend the course of the proceedings in the trial, so as to make a proper defence, and comprehend details of the evidence.'" And it's sourced to the New Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, Oxford University Press, 2000. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is what you were saying there that you have extracted a quotation from the New Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. You're correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is the test you have used to determine whether or not General Strugar --

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: It is not a test. When you say "test," I understand the diagnostic instrument. You mean the trial or question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. This is the standard that the Trial Chamber should apply, is that what you're saying, in determining whether or not General Strugar is fit for trial?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I have quoted from the competent book, from the chapter dealing with forensic issues, how the competency is understood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm asking you: Are you saying - you're the expert here, the professor of psychiatry - telling the Trial Chamber that this is the relevant test that the Trial Chamber should use in assessing General Strugar's fitness?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Again, I can't say it's a test. We obviously understand by "test" something quite different. It's a quotation. It's a paragraph from a relevant European textbook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A definition that the Trial Chamber should refer to?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: This is definition I refer to by being asked to respond to some questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want to do is to show you what the quotation actually says. I want to show you pages -- you, of course, haven't sourced it to a page number. Do you have the page number?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll just show it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If that could be distributed. Distributing page 2091 and 2092 of the New Oxford Textbook on Psychiatry. Could it first be shown to the witness, for time considerations.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have the copy of this text. If it's going to be read, may the interpreters ask for a copy to be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, could you just turn to your left and put it on the overhead projector there. Professor, can you just please read --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would only ask kindly of my learned friend to mark the passage. I cannot see that from the copy I've received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're about to be directed to it, Mr. Petrovic, so just wait a minute and I think all will be revealed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, could you please go to the section in the bottom of the right-hand page -- right hand of page 2091.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under the definition of fitness to stand trial.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just read the paragraph down to the footnote, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: You want me to read aloud?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: "Defendants facing criminal trials need the ability to understand and participate in the proceedings. Psychiatric disorder can render a person incapable or unfit in relation to trial. In its traditional formulation, the test of unfitness to plead is whether the defendant is of sufficient intellect to comprehend the course of the proceedings in the trial, so as to make a proper defence, to know that he might challenge jurors, and to comprehend details of the evidence."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Stop there. It then goes over the page to look at specific considerations. Now, professor, you agree, don't you, that there is no mention there of the words which you have quoted, namely, "to fully comprehend the course of the proceedings"? That's just not what it says, is it?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: You mean I didn't quote the whole paragraph? Yes, I didn't, because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm saying you've misquoted it. It doesn't say "fully comprehend" anywhere, does it?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not even a paraphrasing, is it? It's just wrong, what you've written.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please tell us what is the edition that my learned friend is quoting from. Is it the same edition, the same textbook? Could you please tell us. Could he please show us the textbook so we can be sure that this is the one that they're quoting from. How can we compare something when we do not know whether it is fit to be compared?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is the 2000 edition, we are told, Mr. Petrovic, which is the one referred to by the witness. Is that right, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, of course if you look over the page there, it sets out a number of specific tests which are used in determining or assessing someone's competency to stand trial, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you look at them, they say "specific considerations include whether the defendant understands what he is charged with." It says that, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: You mean the next page?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's one of the things a psychiatrist should look at in determining whether the accused is fit to stand trial, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: To understand the -- what he's charged with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next part is the nature of the Prosecution evidence. That is also something a psychiatrist must assess in coming to a conclusion that a person is unfit to stand trial, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, but also -- and I had the pleasure of reading the chapter that my colleague Dr. Blum has written. There are few models. One of the models is a medical model in which one psychiatrist or doctor should deal with, and these are the emotional, psychiatric conditions and also the overall health of the individual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, I said one of the things. I'm listing the things according to the book you've described as the major English textbook on psychiatry in which you have written a textbook.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the things --

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: That's one of the things, yes. I would agree that that's only one of the things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the -- the next thing is the nature of the Prosecution evidence and the difference between a plea of guilty and not guilty. A psychiatrist must be able to work out whether or not the person understands the -- whether-- a plea of guilty or not guilty, mustn't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whether or not the defendant is able to follow the proceedings. That's also listed.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whether or not the person is able to instruct lawyers. So a defence case can be made.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is also listed there, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is one of the things a competent psychiatrist should determine or assess in coming to a conclusion that a person is unfit to stand trial, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Okay, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you'll note, of course, that Dr. -- Professor Matthews and Dr. Blum addressed each of those things in their report, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: They did refer to each of those things, but they didn't refer to many other things to which I refer to as a doctor and psychiatrist. And as I said on a few occasions today, a psychiatrist is a doctor who should have and give an integrated picture of the person he's dealing with. Because we can't define and diagnose a person only on the ability to stand trial. And I was asked, one of the major questions I was asked, was to evaluate the overall health, including the psychiatric health of the defendant Mr. Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Professor, you have referred to the specific section in the New Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, the definition of fitness, but then you haven't gone on in your report to explore the specific considerations, have you?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: No, because I was following the medical model and made a few -- many diagnoses, somatic and psychiatric, which I thought are very important for Mr. Strugar, who is, I would repeat here, as I said in my report, a seriously ill person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Strugar, of course, gave a very different history to Professor Matthews, Dr. Blum, and Dr. Smalc, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand what kind of different history. What -- could you remind me what is different?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your conclusion is that General Strugar has almost no memory of the war and cannot remember important names. That's your conclusion, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: That was my conclusion, and that was something I was -- the information I was given by his son also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is his son following the trial, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: No. His son is the informant who knows his father very well, and he knows details about his life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The concept of understanding and following a trial, that means, doesn't it, someone following the testimony given in the trial and understanding its effect, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if the general is able to describe in some detail evidence which has been given against him not just that day but over the preceding days, that would indicate that he has the ability to understand and follow the trial, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I'm not sure I could agree with you, because what is important for the condition, somatic and psychiatric, of Mr. Strugar is that it has so-called step-wise fashion, which means that the condition of the defendant is changing, as it is changing of all of us. We are not of the same concentration today as we were yesterday, and neither will we be tomorrow. It depends on many factors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A decision an accused has to make in facing trial is choice of lawyers, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Sorry? The decision?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An accused has to choose lawyers, unless they're court-appointed, to assist in the defence of their case, don't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: As far as I understand the thing, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a choice of lawyers, you would agree, is important for an accused.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Like the choice of many other important persons in one's life, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you are able to choose lawyers, that indicates that you have an ability to -- I withdraw that. A choice of lawyers, who one is fluent in English and the other one is an experienced military lawyer, that's what General Strugar did, he chose a military lawyer and Mr. Petrovic who speaks fluent English; you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know, did he choose them --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: -- on his own will --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: -- or he was advised?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. If you accept that he did that, would you agree that he is exercising a capacity to defend himself?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, again, that I could agree with you, because even the person who is demented can make choices, unless it is the final stage of dementia, when one doesn't recognise anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Someone who has voluntarily surrendered because they say they're innocent and they've come voluntarily to explain that they're not guilty, must understand the difference between a guilty and not guilty plea, mustn't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. A moderately intelligent person, even one who is mentally retarded, who has IQ about 80, would understand these things. It's nothing special.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Someone who can tell psychiatrists that I cannot be guilty, I made sure that I am not guilty and I saved Dubrovnik --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- I was the third commander, Jokic is guilty, not me, certainly shows a capacity to understand the evidence and the trial proceedings; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Again, I'm not sure I could -- it's not a factor that is determined by the overall condition of someone. Even someone who is much sicker could think that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Someone who is able to describe the number of counts on the indictment and the reduction from 17 counts to 5 because "the lawyers persuaded the Court and the charges were reduced," certainly shows a capacity to understand the nature of the charges against them, don't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but if someone is deeply, emotionally related to a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. subject, and that certainly is the accusation and the process that is being here, and if that is being repeated on many occasions, everyone would remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are, of course, no tests or criteria in the SCL-90-R in relation to trial competency, are there?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are no criteria set out in the SCL-90-R related to trial competency, are there?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: No, but there are criteria related to the health of the person who is being examined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because they're not there, I suggest that they are irrelevant to a determination of whether someone is unfit to stand trial in the sense of understanding the nature of the case, the evidence, and being able to instruct counsel.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: If you say that someone who is depressed and who has on the questionnaire you have just quoted, SCL-R, has high level of many clinical syndromes, much higher than the psychiatric in-patient population and non-patients, if you say that this, together with many other diseases that a person has is not relevant, then that is what you said, your responsibility, not mine. My responsibility is only to the science and my profession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, Doctor, did not explore with General Strugar his understanding of whether he was charged with a crime, did you?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask him whether or not he understood that the Court will decide on guilt or innocence?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is it in your report?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I didn't put it, because I wasn't asked to put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about that the trial could result in punishment? Did you explore that with the general?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. He was -- he said on many occasions when he was asked that, that he would commit suicide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is that in your report, about punishment?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: If he gets a sentence, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the various ways a defendant may plead? Did you discuss that with the general?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: No I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about that certain sentences are possible? Did you discuss that with the general?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I didn't. I didn't have time. If I had three or four days, I would discuss it. I was concentrating on the health of General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to list some other things here, to save time, and they're basically in the Prosecution report. Just give me yes or no. The roles of various participants in the trial process. Did you discuss it with him or not? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The general process of the trial. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: You may go with no, because I was concentrating, as I said, on the seriously disturbed health of General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree, wouldn't you, that if the Prosecution -- if what the Prosecution has said in its report -- sorry, what the psychiatrists engaged by the Prosecution have said in their report about the general's ability to understand the proceedings, instruct counsel, enter a plea, and so on, is correct, that he fulfils the competency requirements as set out in the New Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry? You would agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: That's what you said. I wouldn't agree. I can't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Petrovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Lecic, very briefly, just a few questions. In your work, is it typical, is it typical to rely on an additional source of information and interview family members? Is it a legitimate and typical method used in order to obtain information?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I already said, it's a must. It's so-called third ear. And each student, if -- can't pass examination if doesn't rely upon this information, or should at least say that it's very important, so-called heteroanamnesis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My second question: The essence of the role of a psychiatrist, is it to objectivise the information collected from all sources? Is it the essence of your role that, and not just to take information as granted but rather to objectivise it through scientific and professional means at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is the most important factor for every medical profession, including the science that I have devoted myself to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this information you received from General Strugar and from other sources, is it your role to objectivise them, all of the information, in order to write up the report that you have written?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: That was my goal, to ensure that the report is as objective as possible, because my wholly obligation is that to my profession, that is my duty first and foremost.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reason and the criteria that a defendant before the Tribunal might use in selecting his attorneys and those reasons and criteria being that one of the attorneys is experienced in military affairs and the other one speaks English, do you believe that these are legitimate, logical reasons and criteria to use in selecting an attorney?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question. I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My learned friend wanted to demonstrate that General Strugar is able to actively participate in planning his defence and said that he chose two criteria in selecting his attorneys, one being that one speaks English and the other one being that one of them has military experience.

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Do you mean whether this reflects on somebody's psychiatric condition?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I have in mind is: Does this demonstrate that the accused is passive, that the accused lacks interest, and so on?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: I've already said that General Strugar is passive, lacks interest, and has regressed to a helpless state. But what I think is important is that you mentioned yourself, which is that findings need to be objectivised. I do that in my everyday work and I especially do that when preparing a serious report, such as this one. The other issue is whether any other report which does not use the objective measures and whether it can be measured if the author of the report was not objective.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your report, in your report dated 2nd February 2004, did you reply to all of the questions that were mentioned by my learned friend? Let me just quote them: Whether the accused is able to understand the accusations, whether he's able to understand the proceedings, whether he's able to contact and give instructions to his attorneys? Did you write about all of these issues, both in your main report and in your addendum?

utterances.speaker: DUSICA LECIC-TOSEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, indeed, Mr. Petrovic. May we thank you very much, Professor, for your assistance, the work you've done, the report and the supplementary report we've had, and for your being here today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are, of course, now able to return wherever you wish to go. We will adjourn now, and you can then make your arrangements. And the next witness will be in place when we return.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctor. Welcome to the Tribunal. If I could ask you to take the card that is offered to you now and to take the affirmation on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you could please get yourself comfortable. And Mr. Weiner will ask you a few questions to start with. Examined by Mr. Weiner:

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first may I apologise. I'm the one who has caused this five minutes' late problem here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it's taken off your time, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll move fast. What exactly is the time? Is it a total of 25 minutes to be split or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: 25 between evidence in chief and re-examination, your call as to how to break it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that's actually now 24 minutes as a penalty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning. Could you state your name, please.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Daryl Matthews.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where do you live?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Honolulu, Hawaii.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you're employed.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I'm a professor of psychiatry at the University of Hawaii school of medicine and the director of the forensic psychiatry programme at the University of Hawaii.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, what is forensic psychiatry?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Forensic psychiatry is a subspecialty of psychiatry that has the goal of using psychiatry to answer questions that are posed by the legal system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it different from the other areas of psychiatry or the other specialties?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, it has a different focus than the other specialties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does it involve tests and evaluations, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Such as competency, criminal responsibility type of tests?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes, those are some of the major ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever evaluated people as to their competency or criminal responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many persons have you evaluated as to competency or criminal responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Several hundred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on these occasions, who retained you to interview or to evaluate these persons?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: In a great majority of cases, I was a court-appointed evaluator, and in the remainder I was retained either by the Defence or the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you involved at this time in another case in a war-related matter?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where are you involved, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I am an expert for the Defence in a case involving an inmate at the detention facility at Guantanamo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In this case you've been retained by the UN and did you evaluate General Strugar as to his fitness to stand trial or his competency?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a result of that evaluation, did you and two other doctors prepare a report?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have each of you three doctors agreed to that report?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: We have, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you some questions about the interview you had with the accused over a day and a half, two-day period. Did you and the other two doctors question him during those interviews?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during those interviews, did he have any trouble understanding the questions that were asked?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he respond to those questions?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were his answers responsive?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever become confused or disoriented during the interviews?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he show any signs of hallucinations or delusions?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: No, none at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you stated on page 8 of your report that he is inclined to make jokes and give anecdotes. What did you mean by that -- or actually, what was the importance of that, or significance of that?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: We were trying to describe his demeanour, and his demeanour was a cordial one and one which showed a certain amount of flexibility or ability to go from a serious mood state to a somewhat more light-hearted one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what significance does that have as to depression?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: The most seriously depressed individuals don't make jokes, are not able to make jokes, so it would go to the severity of depression, I would say. It would indicate that any depression that he would have would not be the most profound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also indicate on page 15, you said: "He described having read and understood articles and legal documents surrounding the trial." Could you tell us what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: We asked him if he was interested in the proceedings, if he had gotten copies of the various legal documents, if he looked at them and went over them with his attorneys, and he said he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what significance does that have with relation to competency?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: It indicates, at least from what he says, that he is engaged in the process of understanding his case, engaged in the process of assisting counsel, and presumably can understand the documents that he's reading.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You further indicate that during the interview, on page 8, he actively questions the examiners. Could you tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: He asked us questions about our background and the like in an assertive and -- way that is normal in a conversation, perhaps not all that normal in a forensic interview, but seemed reasonable in light of the fact that this is a very high status defendant, and in defendants who are not of high status, they might not be as forward in questioning an examiner, but he felt comfortable doing that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would a passive person actively question the examiners? Would that usually happen?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: No. It would not happen, and his behaviour in terms of the examination was not at all passive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You further state in that same paragraph on page 8: "When explaining certain concepts or events, he is quite elaborate, inclined to precision, and places himself in the role of an educator." What if anything does that indicate as to his intelligence and his memory?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Our impression was that he was quite intelligent and that he is used to explaining complex issues to subordinates and colleagues and others, and that that was a style that he's familiar with and comfortable with, and he continued to do that in the exam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, speaking of the accused's memory, during the interview, did he have any trouble describing the events of 1991?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: We did not detect any trouble describing -- his describing events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any trouble describing his defence or his defence strategy?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the interview, he mentioned about four, maybe five Prosecution witnesses. Did he have any trouble recalling their testimony or what he perceived to be the weaknesses in their testimony?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: No. In fact, he went right to what he perceived was the weakness in their testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also indicate, on page 12: "During the course of the current assessment, Mr. Strugar reminded the interviewers of comments he had made earlier regarding his wife's health, his children's state of employment, discussions he had had with the Prosecution regarding the possibility of a plea agreement, and the nature and history of the command of the unit he ultimately led. He remembered comments made by the interviewers." And there's a quote: "You asked me why I turned myself in." As well as the testimony given during the hearings. Could you tell us about that, what -- could you give us some more information and what exactly happened that you included that paragraph in your statement -- in your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: One of the relevant factors in trial competency, of course, is a person's ability to recall testimony, to recall what might have been said in an earlier conversation and then use that information in subsequent conversations. And he demonstrated that quite well. He did bring up on his own, and also when questioned by us, things that we had discussed earlier. In fact, I recall a time when I myself had forgotten that I had asked him something earlier, and he reminded me that I had asked him that thing earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does that say with relation to both his short-term and long-term memory?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: It says they are quite intact. They are not necessarily perfect or flawless, but they're certainly adequate for the purposes that he was applying to, to discussions of the material that he was discussing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, Doctor, you reviewed certain videotapes of General Strugar in the courtroom. Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Our practice was to try to develop as many sources of information as we could, and certainly to actually see him relate to the Court and to see him in a situation that would be as analogous to testimony as could be, that was very helpful to us and figured into our decision making.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you learn from his statements in the courtroom or in a courtroom setting?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: He was able to speak clearly, coherently, answer the Court's questions appropriately, with good decorum, with some eloquence even. He was perfectly able to communicate in that context, as far as I could tell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also spoke with some of the guards at the Detention Unit. Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Once again, we were trying to develop as many sources of information about General Strugar's mental health as we could and these were people who had spent a fair bit of time with him recently, or at least had enough contact with him that they might have an opinion about his mental condition. So we did query them for that reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you learn from them?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: We learned that my recollection is that two of them found that he had some slight memory difficulties, but their perception was that they were the normal memory difficulties that an elderly person might have and they did not impair his ability to function within the facility, to deal adequately with personnel, to take care of his activities of daily living and the like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Defence psychiatrist indicates that she didn't have any experience with prisoners in gaol, direct experience. Do you have any experience with prisoners in gaol?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you explain the extent. How many years have you interviewed prisoners in gaol, in a gaol setting?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I've been working with people in gaol settings in one capacity or another for about 30 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does gaol affect one's mental behaviour?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: It certainly affects one's mental condition, yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How does it affect? What have you learned? What are some of the different factors that you have seen, or features that you've seen how it affects a person's behaviour or actions?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Depression is enormously common in institutional populations, and people who are in gaols, in prisons, and in other settings where they are deprived of a great deal of their usual comforts and social supports, and the various kinds of depressive symptoms that Mr. Strugar complained of are really quite common in gaol and prison inmates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you said certain kinds of problems, are you talking about loss of appetite, trouble sleeping, or becoming emotional when discussing one's family?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've seen that before in other prisoners that you've interviewed over the past 30 years in gaols?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes, very commonly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very quickly: Are family members objective sources of information?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: They're not normally objective sources of information, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Because they are likely to share goals and hopes with the individual, and they may share them to such a degree that they would be prone to distort information in order to help accomplish those goals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated that -- or in your report, that you followed the evaluation or you used the competency evaluation from Professor Griso [phoen], evaluating competency, forensic assessments and instruments. Is that system of evaluating competency or fitness for trial commonly used?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that Griso's second edition of his competency book, the one that we used and referenced, is as thorough and up-to-date and detailed a discussion of competency issues in forensic mental health that exists in the English language and so that's the reason we chose that book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I would like you to look at this document, sir. Just very briefly: Are those the Griso factors?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you mention each of those factors in your report?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd like to offer that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, is there any requirement that you're aware of that an accused must fully comprehend the course of the proceedings in a trial in order to be fit to stand trial and in order to be competent?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: No, there's no such requirement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And since we're talking about requirements, have you been involved in establishing the competency tests and requirements in the United States, or standards?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I've been involved in developing the protocols for competency evaluations by psychiatrists as part of the American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law, which is the forensic psychiatry professional association. They're promulgating guidelines in how to do trial competency evaluations and I've been part of that effort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the University of Hawaii and in your lectures around the world, do you teach the standards and the tests to be used in determining competency?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And based on your experience, there is no requirement to fully comprehend the course of the proceedings in this trial; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, there was some discussion concerning the degrees of dementia. In your opinion, are there various degrees of dementia?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes, there are various degrees of dementia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please explain to the Court your belief or opinion as to the various degrees, why there are various degrees.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Anybody who has had the sad experience of having a relative suffer from Alzheimer's disease, which is the most common cause of dementia, would recognise that the disease starts off with very, very mild kinds of difficulties, perhaps forgetting names or where you put your keys, and over the course of many years, progresses to the point where there may be total inability to remember even the loved ones that surround that person, and a total inability to function to the extent that they may have to be institutionalised. And so there's certainly a great spectrum of severity in dementia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And utilising a spectrum, where would General Strugar's level of dementia be?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Mr. Strugar's level of dementia is mild. There are some indicators that it might not even be present, but on balance, I think the best estimation of his mentation is that he has a mild degree of dementia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can a person with mild dementia be competent or fit to stand trial?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes, they surely can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can a person with mild dementia be competent or fit to carry on with their everyday life?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, are you familiar with post-traumatic stress disorder?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever assessed anyone as to whether or not they have post-traumatic stress disorder?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many times have you assessed persons for that problem?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: My estimate would be 50 to 100 people who were either coming to me for treatment, when I had a treatment practice, or who I was evaluating for forensic reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever treated persons recently with post-traumatic stress disorder?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I haven't treated anybody since 1990, I believe. That was the last.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
