utterances.text: But have you evaluated anyone recently for post-traumatic stress disorder?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I've evaluated people as recently as this year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you evaluate General Strugar to determine if he had post-traumatic stress disorder?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were your findings, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: We did not identify post-traumatic stress disorder. He did not report to us the range of symptoms that would be required to have post-traumatic stress disorder. So we did not diagnose that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even if you reach this diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder, would it have made any difference?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: No, not in and of itself. Diagnosis per se, no matter what the diagnosis is, does not speak directly to the question of competence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, the Defence psychiatrist performed a number of tests, a depression test, an IES test, an SCL-90 test, a Beck and Hamilton test. What relevance do these tests have to competency?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: They're not relevant, they have no relevance to trial competency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Competency is a functional ability and it has to do with what one is able to do and what one isn't able to do. Those various tests refer to individuals' reports of their own feeling states. So they're quite helpful in assessment for purposes of treatment, so if one were involved in treating people who had been subject to trauma, certainly those kind of tests are very relevant. But in medical-legal assessments, they don't have any place. They're not used ever, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Weiner. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. May I ask for the lectern, please. It would make my life much easier. Cross-examined by Mr. Petrovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Dr. Matthews. I will ask you a couple of questions regarding your report and your testimony today. Tell us first of all, please, have you ever evaluated anyone from the territory where the Serbian language is spoken in your practice today?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: No, not previous to this occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever evaluated anyone from that area through an interpreter? Because it is a language you do not understand.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I've never evaluated anyone from that area, with an interpreter or without.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the fact that you evaluated General Strugar through an interpreter affect your conclusions? Does the manner of interpretation have any influence on your conclusions, on your final position?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: It might. That's the reason we conducted the examination, both with a person who spoke the language and with an interpreter as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which diagnosis did you establish in General Strugar's case?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: The only diagnosis that we felt there was sufficient evidence to establish was dementia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us precisely, please, which type of dementia, which form of dementia.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: We diagnosed vascular dementia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see the MRI that was done for General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I saw briefly the film, I think, and then I saw the report as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen the MRI done in March 2004 here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes. I think I didn't see the actual film of the 2004 one; I only saw the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then be so kind as to tell us which report did you see regarding this MRI from 2004.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I would need to look at the list of documents that I reviewed to cite that. The MRI is not something that has any bearing on his competence, so I must tell you that I did not pay a great deal of attention to the MRI.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kindly tell us: Have you seen that MRI report from 2004? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I've seen what Dr. Pressman concluded. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am asking you if you have seen the report, because you just mentioned you did. That's page 89, line 7. Have you seen that report?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I have seen the results that Dr. Pressman reached when he interpreted the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what form did you see the results of Dr. Pressman, the findings of Dr. Pressman?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Perhaps it was a copy of an e-mail from him. We were working on our report and that was the last thing that had not come in yet, was Dr. Pressman's interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Matthews, have you read at all this report that you signed?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I put it to you that you haven't read it, because if you had, you would understand that Dr. Pressman telephoned one of your colleagues to inform them of the contents of the MRI film, which is indicated on several occasions in the report itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection. It's a misreading of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In what respect, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The first four findings were sent by e-mail, the last finding was a discussion over the telephone --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would appreciate it if my learned friend would not testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm not testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That was an answer to my question, Mr. Petrovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- to deal with your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All I wanted to say is it's an improper reading. The first four were sent by an e-mail between the doctors, and the last one is they had telephone conversations because they're all in different states in the United States. This doctor is in Hawaii, one is in Arizona, one is in California, and the fourth one is in Croatia, so they had to use e-mail and telephone calls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you would carry on now, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me. On page 2 of the report Dr. Matthews claims to have read before signing, it says: Examination interviews. 15th March 2004, by telephone, Barry D. Pressman, M.D., 15th March 2004. It doesn't -- telephonic, in brackets. Then the only place on page 4 which refers to the findings of Dr. Pressman regarding the MRI, in paragraph 3, the last sentence again refers to an interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you, Dr. Matthews, before signing this, have not read the report at all, or maybe you've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Well, I would think the latter is more likely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with all the elements of this report?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I believe I'm familiar with it. I haven't committed it to memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the report from a month ago. Do you have any problems in conducting your business if you can't remember what you signed a month ago?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Sir, I have no problems conducting my business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How often do you apply the PARADISE test in your practice?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I don't apply it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this test applied in writing this report?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: The report was drafted different sections by different individuals. Dr. Bennett Blum developed the PARADISE test and used that model in drafting his section of the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why don't -- why are you not applying this test?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: In this case or in other cases?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Generally speaking, because you say you never apply it. So generally speaking, why do you never apply it?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I don't apply it because the majority of my practice is not a geriatric practice, that it's not that common that I do forensic evaluations on elderly people, and Dr. Blum created this with that population in mind. Secondly, there are other methods of getting at the same kinds of results. I think in this case both Blum's model and Griso's model really get to the same kinds of conclusions. So there's --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is the PARADISE test a psychiatric test designed to evaluate trial competency?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To what extent have you in your practice evaluated elderly persons aged 71 in terms of their trial competency? How many such persons did you evaluate?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Probably dozens over the years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does every person you evaluate -- does every person you evaluated suffer from vascular dementia?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What percentage of the population aged 71, in general, suffers from vascular dementia?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago, answering one of my learned friend's questions, you said that depression in General Strugar's case is not the deepest form of depression, the severest form. However, General Strugar does suffer from depression. It is his clinical diagnosis, one of them.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: That is not a diagnosis that we reached. No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you, then, on page 78, line 22, say, a couple of minutes ago, that depression in this man's case is not in its deepest form? This seems to imply that depression does exist.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I would invite you to differentiate between depression as a complaint, as a state of mind, and depression as a medical disorder or psychiatric disorder. People can experience the state of depression, and commonly do, without qualifying for the psychiatric disorder, diagnosis, depression. So I believe that Mr. Strugar has commonly felt depressed, but I don't believe that he has met the diagnostic criteria for any particular psychiatric disorder involving depression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you tried to establish if General Strugar suffers from depression at all? Did you apply any method at all to establish whether depression exists in his case?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe General Strugar when he tells you that he had read all the documents that are relevant to this trial?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: That's a misstatement of my testimony. I did not say that he had read or told me that he had read all of the documents relevant to this trial. He's read some documents, and I believe him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why do you believe him?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I believe him because throughout our evaluation of him, he did not give any indication of deception. He impressed us all as a straightforward, honest man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he try to hide anything from you, to keep anything from you?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: It's a little hard to know, because if he successfully kept it from us, we wouldn't know that he really had it. But it wouldn't surprise me if he minimised his symptoms somewhat. He did want to present himself in a favourable light, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he tell you about the strategy of his defence?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I can refer to my report and tell you what he said to me. He said he had a written order to show the Court, had to do with an instruction he gave not to fire on Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's all he told you about his defence strategy?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I don't know that that's all he told me. That's the one thing I put my eye on the minute you asked me that question. I can spend time looking through the report, see if there are others. Also, I can obtain my notes and go through those and see if there are others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he mention any concept of defence, any plan of defence, from all the discussions in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he present to you any concept of defence? Not only whether he had a paper or not; did he tell you how he intended to approach his defence, how he intended to speak before the Court, what he was planning, what he was planning to say?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I recall that he said that he had gotten there later than the people who were really involved in doing this and that he himself was not involved. I don't remember the details of his proposed defence, however.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When analysing the videotapes and transcripts -- in fact, tell me first: Who made a selection of these tapes? I don't believe you have seen the entire amount of tapes available at this moment, because this is a very long proceeding.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: We were interested in tapes in which Mr. Strugar actually spoke to the Court, so we certainly didn't see the entire tape of all the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, on any one of those occasions, hear him say anything that does not refer to tea or his neck or similar things? Did you find anything in what he was saying that did not refer to his health alone?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I know he wasn't talking about the war at the time, but what he did talk about, he was able to talk about just fine and was able to remember past episodes of medical care, past insults to his health. So his conversation seemed to be coherent and normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 11 and 12 of your report, as evidence of his ability to remember information, you quote exclusively his medical history. Do you have any other evidence that he is indeed able to memorise new information and to recall old information?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: What does it mean to you, after observing him for an hour in this courtroom, when he spent more than an hour with his eyes closed here, sleeping in the courtroom? What does that tell you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. That is a valid objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The fact that his eyes are closed doesn't mean he's sleeping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I've said it was a valid objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it mean to you, the fact that you have been watching him for an hour and that perhaps half of that time he had his eyes closed? How do you interpret that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Doctor, whether, when you were watching, the eyes of the accused were closed for any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you referring to the observation period we had when he was in Court rather than right now? I'm not sure what counsel is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think he's referring to the time you spent observing the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His eyes were closed sometimes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Petrovic will ask you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long and what is your conclusion? What is the cause of this? Just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: The most interesting is that when there was something came up that interested him, he would open his eyes, that he was listening, and he could differentiate between topics that were being talked about by the witness, and when the topic was of interest to him, he was able to open his eyes and attend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you think that he is able to distinguish between what is interesting and important as opposed to other things. Do you think that what is important for the proceedings is also important and interesting for him, and then he opens his eyes and attends?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: That was my impression, yes, that when they were talking about -- when the witness was talking about personal matters and things that upset her, those were the times that he was likely to keep his eyes closed, and when she began talking about things that came closer to military topics that he might have had some knowledge or involvement in, then he opened his eyes and paid attention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, in one sentence, tell me: What did that witness testify about when you were here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: She was testifying about her property being damaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he find interesting in her testimony, and what did he find without interest?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: My recollection is that when she was describing her property and the suffering she experienced, he was less interested than -- he was less interested than when he was talking about shelling and damage and military activities that were going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You say in your report that he has retained many cognitive functions, on page 13, paragraph 1. What cognitive functions has he lost?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: He has some mild memory impairment, and I'll say again, it is mild. He has some mild word-finding difficulties. He has difficulty at times coming up with a word. There's controversy in the mental health field as to whether word-finding difficulties are a memory problem or a language problem. If you consider them a memory problem, then he would not qualify for the diagnosis of dementia. We essentially gave him or the seriousness of his condition the benefit of the doubt and took the word-finding difficulties to be a separate symptom, and so he did qualify for the diagnosis of dementia. Still, the word-finding difficulties were not of such severity that any of us would have called it, for example, an expressive aphasia, which is a major neurologic problem, and his cognitive functioning was not that far from normal. He only had mild impairments. There was nothing beyond that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe that there is a classification of vascular dementia; mild, moderate, and grave one? Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: No, I'm not claiming that there's an official classification. I'm claiming that in nature, there exists mild dementias and serious dementias. Whether or not medicine has developed a classification for it is not what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What test have you applied? What standard have you applied to determine that this is a mild case and not a serious one?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: We have first looked at the various prior evaluations he had, so for example, the Military Medical Academy diagnosed his dementia essentially as mild, and I believe there are other prior evaluations that found that any cognitive impairment he had is mild. We found his cognitive impairments to be mild; we didn't find any impairments that exceeded that in degree of severity, and so then it's hard to imagine how his total condition then could be something more serious than mild.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, you did not apply any specific scale. This is just a finding that you reached based on your impression?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: We did not apply any specific scale. We used our impressions and the impressions of others that had evaluated him previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 17 of your report, paragraph 3, you state that he is considering suicide as a rational option, rational alternative. As a physician, how can you believe suicide to be a rational option, ever, in anybody's case? Or do you, as a physician, claim that for some persons, a suicide may be a rational option?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that for some persons, suicide is a rational option.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, do you recognise or do you see that this patient has this ability to carry out this rational option?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you include the suicide into your concept of rational planning of his strategy? Do you believe that to be part of strategy, part of plan? And if so, do you believe that to be rational?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: No, I don't believe that that's part of his strategy. I think that he spoke of suicide should his defence fail. And the circumstances that he spoke of, yes, it might be rational under his circumstances to commit suicide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What circumstances would those be where you would believe that to be a rational solution for his circumstances? I'm asking you this as a physician.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Well, when you say you're asking me this as a physician, then I start becoming a little bit puzzled. Do you mean do I think that there's something irrational about his thinking? That's the kind of thing I would evaluate as a physician. I don't believe there's anything at all irrational about Mr. Strugar's thinking. I believe that he does not suffer from a serious mood disorder which --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm putting a specific question to you. I'm asking you about suicide because you stated that this is a rational option to spending the rest of his life imprisoned, incarcerated with criminals. So I'm trying to find out what do you find rational about it?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Rationality is not a property of the conclusion. Rationality is a property of the reasoning process used to reached the conclusion. I don't believe there's anything irrational about his mental processes. I believe he's able to look at states of affairs and understand consequences, weigh risks and benefits, look at his own values, and reach a conclusion that's satisfactory to him. So I would say that that's a rational decision-making process. That's the basis upon which I say it's rational.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you include suicide as a solution into his concept of rational decision making? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Not as you say it, no. You've misstated my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Do you claim that somebody who forgets two concepts out of three that were mentioned to him can testify before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I sure do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe that if that person forgets three -- two concepts out of three, that such person can be cross-examined?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: It's a mistake to think that you can look at one of these tests done at one period of time, using three random concepts picked by a particular examiner, and use that alone to reach the conclusion that one may or may not testify. If I've tried to stress anything here, what it is is this is a complex multi-determined process and we try to look at as many different features of his mental condition as possible. And it is extremely oversimplifying our reasoning to say that because he couldn't remember something on one occasion, that that would produce an impairment. That's not our opinion, that's not the way mental health processes work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Somebody who has difficulty remembering events and names, which goes with the vascular dementia, can such person testify in his own case and subject himself to the possibility of not being able to answer a question put by the Prosecutor, not because he doesn't want to but because he cannot remember?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Mr. Strugar's memory impairment was not to the extent that it would impair his ability to testify. He did remember relevant names, as far as we could determine, and when he couldn't remember a name, my recollection is that he would think about it for a while and then recall the name. I don't think he has a serious memory impairment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You think that such a person can testify before the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I don't think that "such a person" can testify; I think that Mr. Strugar can testify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us: If the person cannot remember, for example, your name and the Prosecutor puts that question to him and he is testifying in court, do you believe that to be a problem which can affect his standing before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: No, I don't believe that the fact that he couldn't remember the name of an American psychiatrist who questioned him briefly on a particular day, I don't think that affects his trial competency, I don't think it affects his ability to testify relevantly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, if he cannot remember the name of the witness whom he also saw once in his lifetime for a period of two hours, could that pose a problem to him, if he spent less time with that witness than with you and also cannot remember his name?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: This requires really a lot of speculation to answer the question, and if you'd like me to speculate, I will. Shall I?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Try.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Okay. I think it would depend on how important knowing that name would be. He certainly knew I was an American psychiatrist, he knew I was hired by the Prosecution, he knew that I was going to be evaluating him for purposes of trial competency. All the important stuff he remembered, he knew. It's just the name that he didn't, because the name was not particularly important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Matthews, what if he believes some name not to be important and therefore cannot remember that name, and the OTP believes that name to be crucial, how would he testify under those circumstances in court?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: It's not just Mr. Strugar that has memory problems. Everybody has memory problems. They are very, very common as people age, and having difficulty remembering things during testimony is a problem that many witnesses and defendants have. It certainly is a matter of degree, and I'll say once again that Mr. Strugar's memory difficulties are in the range of someone who has normal memory for his age, up to being mildly demented, that that's the severity of his memory problems. Those people normally are found competent to stand trial and they're normally able to give testimony adequately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, do all of us have a sort of vascular dementia? Do all of us suffer from it? Do all of us have problems with memory? Does Mr. Strugar have problems just like all other people do? Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Which of those would you like me to answer?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All three.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Do all of us have a sort of vascular dementia? No. Do all of us suffer from it? No. Do all of us have problems with memory? Everybody has memory difficulties at some time. Nobody remembers everything that ever happened to them. Does Mr. Strugar have problems just like all other people do? His problems are very much the kinds of memory problems that people develop normally when they age, but maybe they're a little bit worse than that as a result of his vascular disease. I think that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then he and the vascular dementia that he has at age 71, how does he differ from a person of same age who does not suffer from vascular dementia? Could you please give us the answer to that and we'll conclude.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: He doesn't differ very much. He differs a little in that his memory is a little bit worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Weiner, is there any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just briefly. Re-examined by Mr. Weiner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of your report, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you turn to page number 1.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last line. It says medical report -- sorry, medical record/reports. And it lists on page to the persons that they received that from, in putting this report together. Could you tell us what the last name is on that group of reports and records.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Dr. Barry D. Pressman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we look at the next part, it says examinations, interviews, the last name the person -- the last name on that list of persons.

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Barry Pressman, M.D.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was some sort of e-mail or some sort of report by Dr. Pressman that was incorporated in this full report?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: That's my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, they asked you about the PARADISE test. Is that a tool which can be used in determining competency?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes. It's one that is helpful in reaching a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that concerns cognitive functioning, does that not?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that part of a competency evaluation?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, they asked you about mild dementia. The people who see him, who see the accused daily, the people at the Detention Unit, did they complain to you or the other two doctors about any serious problems in relation to the defendant?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they complain to you about any serious memory problems in relation to the defendant?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there was some discussion about his view on suicide. Was that view of suicide linked to conviction?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any other discussion of suicide as if it could occur today, tomorrow, in the next few weeks, or was it solely limited to what he might do if convicted?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: It was solely limited to what he might do if convicted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there was some discussion with regard to honesty in answering questions. Are you referring to honesty in relation to answering questions or honesty in relation to guilt or innocence in this case?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I believe he was honest in answering our questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you indicated that at one point during the testimony of a woman whose property was damaged, he became animated and his eyes opened and he was listening to -- or he appeared to be listening to the testimony. What did it concern at that point?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: I think it concerned the shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he complain to you that he found not all of the information that was coming out from witnesses to be interesting to him?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Yes. He complained about the testimony in that way, and in others, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you find that unusual for defendants or prisoners to state, based on your experience?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Somewhat unusual, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it unusual as to be a medical problem?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: No. I would say that it's unusual in that he was quite focused on the testimony and its accuracy and in finding indicia that it might be inaccurate. I think that it's not a reflection of poor mental condition at all that he was focused in the way he focused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, do you remember reading a transcript, the following transcript, where the accused said -- and this is page 721: "I'm not asking for any leniency. I know exactly where I am. I'm being tried. But I've been listening to something that I've already went through. What happened in Yugoslavia, my Defence counsel, I suppose, will be able to tell that. However, I was really -- it was really necessary for me to listen to all that has been said today. What has that got to do with my indictment?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "What has that got to do with my indictment? Why did I have to listen to that? So much for me." And then he finishes: "Thank you very much." Now, do you find it unusual that certain defendants might not want to listen to certain portions of a trial?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: No, not at all. There may be a great deal of material in a trial that would be very upsetting to a particular defendant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or uninteresting?

utterances.speaker: DARYL MATTHEWS
utterances.text: Or uninteresting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's a document, Mr. Re. I read your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. We're on the same plane. May I tender into evidence the extract of the New Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, 2nd edition, 2000, pages 2091 and 92. Mr. Petrovic is on his feet. I can hand him the front page. I haven't photocopied six copies of the front page, which Dr. Matthews got for me this morning, because the photocopier wasn't working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the Defence please be able to see what this is about before we reply to this request of my learned friend. I don't think we can do it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, it is the two pages that were put to Dr. Lecic from the text that she quoted in her report. They were put to her. We had copies. Mr. Re omitted to tender them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I leave it up to you to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P167. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Also, Your Honour, on the topic of tendering exhibits, although the reports have been filed with the Trial Chamber, it appears that they haven't actually been tendered into evidence on the application. Do Your Honours -- did Your Honours wish to have them tendered formally as exhibits in -- on the application in these proceedings or remaining on the file as reports which have been adopted and referred to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No counsel has sought to tender them. From the point of view of the Chamber, it feels that it may properly consider them and should consider the reports of the doctors that have been called to give evidence. They have been the basis of the questioning, or the questioning has supplemented. If either counsel feels that that may lead to some form of technical deficiency, we would receive them, but we don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution, unfortunately, suspects later on it may well lead to, could possibly, and we would like to offer into evidence the report of our three psychiatrists formally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That report will be received and will the report of Dr. Lecic and its supplement. The numbers will be given when we resume on Monday, because of time constraints at the moment. Could I do two further things in our limited time. Firstly, indicate that the Chamber would like to receive brief, succinct, written submissions on the question of competence to stand trial by the close of our hearing on Tuesday, from each party, and we would indicate that at the close of the evidence of the witness who is presently part heard, we would invite very brief oral submissions to supplement those written submissions. We would think they probably need not exceed ten minutes for each party. And that will be perhaps on Tuesday. Could I thank you, Doctor, for your presence here, the work that you've done to assist us, and your -- the way that you've been able to deal succinctly with a wide range of questions that have been posed to you today. We're grateful for what you have done and wish you well on your journey home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're quite welcome, and thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will now adjourn until Monday afternoon at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 3rd day of May 2004, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
